tutorials.title: The Sieve of Eratosthenes
tutorials.body: The Sieve of Eratosthenes is an ancient trick for finding every prime up to some number without dividing at all. Write all the numbers from 2 onward, then circle 2 and cross off every multiple of 2; circle the next uncrossed number (3) and cross off all its multiples; keep going. Whatever is left circled is prime. It is like a colander straining out the composites and leaving the primes behind, and it is far faster than testing each number one at a time.

tutorials.title: How a Factor Tree Works
tutorials.body: A factor tree is a step-by-step way to find a number's prime factorization. Start with your number and split it into any two factors that multiply to it, then keep splitting each branch until every tip is a prime. For example, 36 splits into 6 and 6; each 6 splits into 2 and 3, so the tree ends in 2, 2, 3, 3. No matter which split you pick first, you always land on the same set of primes at the bottom.

tutorials.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
tutorials.body: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says that every whole number greater than 1 is either prime or can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way, ignoring the order. This is why primes are called the building blocks of numbers, like atoms that combine to form every molecule. For example, 90 is always 2 times 3 times 3 times 5, and you can never find a different bundle of primes that also multiplies to 90. That guarantee of uniqueness is what makes factoring so powerful.

tutorials.title: Factors and Divisors
tutorials.body: A factor (also called a divisor) of a number is any whole number that divides it evenly, leaving no remainder. Factors always come in pairs that multiply to the original number. For example, the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12, because 1 times 12, 2 times 6, and 3 times 4 all hit 12 exactly. A handy real-world version: the factors of 12 are all the ways you could share 12 cookies into equal groups with none left over.

tutorials.title: The Euclidean Algorithm
tutorials.body: The Euclidean algorithm is a fast, ancient way to find the greatest common factor without listing any factors. You divide the bigger number by the smaller and keep only the remainder, then repeat with the smaller number and that remainder, again and again until the remainder hits zero; the last nonzero remainder is the GCF. For example, for 48 and 18: 48 leaves remainder 12, then 18 leaves remainder 6, then 12 leaves remainder 0, so the GCF is 6. It is dramatically quicker than factoring when the numbers are large.

tutorials.title: What Are Twin Primes?
tutorials.body: Twin primes are a pair of prime numbers that sit just two apart, with a single number squeezed between them. Examples include 3 and 5, 11 and 13, and 17 and 19. As you count higher, primes spread out and twins get rarer, yet mathematicians keep finding enormous ones. Whether twin primes go on forever is still an unsolved mystery called the Twin Prime Conjecture, one of the famous open questions in math.

tutorials.title: What Is a Perfect Number?
tutorials.body: A perfect number is a number that exactly equals the sum of all its divisors smaller than itself. The first one is 6: its proper divisors are 1, 2, and 3, and 1 plus 2 plus 3 equals 6. The next is 28, since 1 plus 2 plus 4 plus 7 plus 14 also adds back up to 28. Perfect numbers are surprisingly rare and have fascinated mathematicians since ancient Greece, where they were seen as numbers in perfect balance with their own parts.

tutorials.title: Why Anything to the Zero Power Is One
tutorials.body: Any number (except zero itself) raised to the power of zero equals one. Here's the idea: each time you lower the exponent by one, you divide by the base. So going from the base squared to the base to the first power, you divide once; go down one more step to the zero power and you divide again, which lands you on one. It's like climbing down a staircase by dividing each step, and the step labeled zero always sits at one.

tutorials.body: A decimal is a way of writing numbers that aren't whole by using a dot called a decimal point. The digits after the point stand for parts of one: tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths, getting ten times smaller each step. When you pay $3.50 for a sandwich, the 3 is three whole dollars and the .50 is fifty hundredths of a dollar, which is fifty cents. It always has the same straight-line shape when you graph it. Think of a taxi fare: a flat fee plus a steady rate per mile is a linear equation, like cost = base + rate times miles. Imagine your phone bill is a fee plus a charge times the gigabytes used; to find the gigabytes you first subtract the fee, then divide by the charge. tutorials.body: An equation is like a balance scale with the equals sign as the pivot point: both sides weigh exactly the same. If you add, subtract, multiply, or divide one side, you must do the identical thing to the other side or the scale tips and the statement stops being true. Picture two bags that weigh the same; if you drop a rock in one bag, you have to drop an identical rock in the other to keep them even. tutorials.title: Flipping the Inequality Sign
tutorials.body: When you multiply or divide both sides of an inequality by a negative number, the inequality symbol must reverse direction to stay true. The reason is that negatives turn the number line backwards: the bigger a number's size, the more negative and therefore smaller it becomes. For example five is greater than three, but multiply both by negative one and you get negative five, which is actually less than negative three. Forgetting this flip is the number one inequality mistake.

tutorials.title: What Is a Compound Inequality?
tutorials.body: A compound inequality joins two inequality conditions into one statement, using the word and when both must be true at once or the word or when either one is enough. An and statement traps the variable between two bounds, like saying a comfortable room temperature is at least sixty-eight degrees and at most seventy-two degrees. An or statement covers two separate stretches, such as being too cold below sixty or too hot above eighty. Graphing it shows either a single band in the middle or two separate shaded regions.

tutorials.title: Acute, Right, Obtuse, and Straight Angles
tutorials.body: An angle measures how much you turn between two lines that meet at a point, counted in degrees. A right angle is exactly 90 degrees, like the square corner of a piece of paper. An acute angle is smaller than that (sharp, like a slice of pizza), an obtuse angle is bigger than 90 but less than 180 (a wide-open laptop lid), and a straight angle is exactly 180 degrees, a flat line. Think of a clock: at 3 o'clock the hands make a right angle, and as the minute hand keeps going the angle opens up.

tutorials.title: Complementary and Supplementary Angles
tutorials.body: Two angles are complementary when they add up to 90 degrees, and supplementary when they add up to 180 degrees. So if one angle is 30 degrees, its complement is 60 and its supplement is 150. A handy memory trick: 'C' comes before 'S' in the alphabet, and 90 comes before 180. Picture cutting a square corner into two pieces, those pieces are complementary; lay an angle along a straight line and the leftover is its supplement.

tutorials.title: Why a Triangle's Angles Add to 180
tutorials.body: The three inside angles of any flat triangle always add up to 180 degrees, no matter the shape. You can feel why with a paper triangle: tear off all three corners and place them tip-to-tip, and they line up into a perfectly straight line, which is 180 degrees. This means if you know two angles you can always find the third by subtracting from 180. It's why a triangle can have at most one right angle or one obtuse angle, never two.

tutorials.title: Equilateral, Isosceles, and Scalene Triangles
tutorials.body: Triangles are named by how many sides have equal length. An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal and all three angles equal to 60 degrees, like a road yield sign. An isosceles triangle has two equal sides and two equal base angles, like the classic shape of a slice of cheese. A scalene triangle has all three sides different lengths, with no two angles the same. You can also name triangles by their angles: right, acute, or obtuse.

tutorials.title: Polygons and Their Names
tutorials.body: A polygon is a closed flat shape made of straight sides, with no curves and no gaps. They're named by their number of sides: a triangle has 3, a quadrilateral 4, a pentagon 5, a hexagon 6, an octagon 8. You see them everywhere, a stop sign is an octagon and a honeybee's comb is built from hexagons because they tile without leaving gaps. A polygon is 'regular' when all its sides and angles are equal, like a perfect snowflake's six-pointed frame.

tutorials.title: Squares, Rectangles, Rhombuses, and Other Quadrilaterals
tutorials.body: A quadrilateral is any four-sided polygon, and the family has special members. A rectangle has four right angles, a rhombus has four equal sides, and a square is both at once, four equal sides AND four right angles, like a floor tile. A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides that lean, like a pushed-over rectangle, and a trapezoid has just one pair of parallel sides, like a lampshade seen from the side. Every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square.

tutorials.title: Radius, Diameter, and the Parts of a Circle
tutorials.body: A circle is the set of all points the same distance from a center point. The radius is the distance from the center to the edge, and the diameter is the full distance straight across through the center, which is always exactly twice the radius. The circumference is the distance all the way around the rim, like the length of string it would take to wrap a coin. A chord is any straight line connecting two points on the edge, and the longest possible chord is the diameter.

tutorials.title: What Pi Means
tutorials.body: Pi is the number you get when you divide any circle's circumference (the distance around) by its diameter (the distance across), and amazingly it's the same for every circle, about 3.14. So no matter how big or small the circle, going around is always a little more than three times going across. You can test it by wrapping a string around a can, then comparing it to three widths of the can, you'll have a bit left over. Pi never ends and never repeats, which is why we round it.

tutorials.title: Perimeter Versus Area
tutorials.body: Perimeter is the distance all the way around the outside of a shape, measured in plain length units like meters. Area is the amount of flat space inside the shape, measured in square units like square meters. Imagine a garden: the perimeter is the length of fence you need to surround it, and the area is the amount of grass you'd lay inside. Two shapes can share the same perimeter but have very different areas, which is why a square encloses more space than a long skinny rectangle of the same fence length.

tutorials.title: Congruent and Similar Shapes
tutorials.body: Two shapes are congruent when they are exactly the same size and shape, so one could be slid, turned, or flipped to land perfectly on top of the other, like two cutouts from the same cookie cutter. Two shapes are similar when they have the same shape but different sizes, like a photo and its enlarged poster, the angles match but the lengths are scaled up or down by the same factor. So all congruent shapes are also similar, but similar shapes are only congruent when the scale factor is exactly 1.

tutorials.title: Parallel and Perpendicular Lines
tutorials.body: Parallel lines run in the same direction and stay exactly the same distance apart forever, so they never cross, like the two rails of a train track. Perpendicular lines cross each other to form a right angle, a perfect 90-degree corner, like the lines where a wall meets the floor. A quick test: a capital letter L shows perpendicular lines, while the two long sides of a ladder show parallel lines. Both ideas describe how straight lines relate, either side by side or meeting squarely.

tutorials.title: Lines of Symmetry and Rotational Symmetry
tutorials.body: A shape has reflection symmetry when you can fold it along a line and the two halves match exactly, like folding a heart down the middle. That fold line is called the line of symmetry, and some shapes have several, a square has four. A shape has rotational symmetry when you can spin it around its center and it looks the same before completing a full turn, like a pinwheel or a starfish. Butterflies, snowflakes, and faces are full of symmetry, which is part of why we find them pleasing to look at.

tutorials.title: Interior and Exterior Angles of Polygons
tutorials.body: The interior angles are the corners inside a polygon, and their total grows in a steady pattern: a triangle's add to 180, a quadrilateral's to 360, and each extra side adds another 180 degrees. The reason is that any polygon can be sliced from one corner into triangles, and each triangle contributes its 180. The exterior angles, the turns you'd make walking around the outside, always add to a full 360 degrees no matter how many sides, just like a person walking once around a city block ends up facing their starting direction again.

tutorials.title: What Is Area?
tutorials.body: Area is the amount of flat space a shape covers, measured in square units like square inches or square meters. Imagine tiling a floor with little square tiles that are each one unit on a side: the area is just how many of those tiles it takes to cover the whole surface with no gaps or overlaps. That's why area is always written with a little 2, like cm², since you are counting squares. A bigger room needs more tiles, so it has a bigger area.

tutorials.title: Radius and Diameter

The diameter is the distance all the way across the circle passing through the center, which is exactly two radii laid end to end. So the diameter is always twice the radius. Picture a wheel: the radius is a single spoke from the hub to the rim, and the diameter is a full line straight across through the middle.

tutorials.title: What Is Volume?
tutorials.body: Volume is the amount of three-dimensional space something takes up, or how much it can hold inside, measured in cubic units like cubic centimeters. If area is about covering a flat floor with squares, volume is about filling a box with little unit cubes and counting them. That is why volume uses a little 3, like cm³. A moving truck holds more boxes than a shoebox because it has far more volume.

For a box, you find the area of each of the six flat faces and add them all up. Picture wrapping a present: the surface area is how much wrapping paper it takes to cover the whole box. Surface area uses square units, while volume measures the space inside.

tutorials.title: Area of Compound Shapes
tutorials.body: A compound or irregular shape is one made by joining simpler shapes together, like an L-shaped room. To find its area, slice it into rectangles and triangles you already know how to handle, find each piece's area, then add them up. tutorials.title: What Is Trigonometry?
tutorials.body: Trigonometry is the study of how the angles and side lengths of triangles connect to each other. The big idea is that in a right triangle, once you fix one angle, the ratios between the sides are locked in no matter how big or small the triangle is. That's why a surveyor can measure the angle up to the top of a mountain and its distance away, then figure out the height without ever climbing it. Trig turns angles you can measure into lengths you can't reach.

tutorials.title: Right Triangles and Their Sides
tutorials.body: A right triangle is any triangle with one square corner of exactly ninety degrees, the kind you see in the corner of a book. The longest side, always sitting opposite that square corner, is called the hypotenuse. The other two sides are named relative to whichever angle you're looking at: the one touching the angle is the adjacent side, and the one across from it is the opposite side. Picture leaning a ladder against a wall: the ladder is the hypotenuse, the wall is one leg, and the ground is the other.

tutorials.title: Sine, Cosine, and Tangent
tutorials.body: Sine, cosine, and tangent are just three ratios you build from the sides of a right triangle, given one of its angles. Sine is the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse, cosine is the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse, and tangent is the opposite divided by the adjacent. Many people memorize this with SOH-CAH-TOA: Sine = Opposite over Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent over Hypotenuse, Tangent = Opposite over Adjacent. If you stand and look up at a kite, the angle of your gaze plus one known distance lets these ratios hand you the kite's height.

tutorials.title: Finding a Missing Side

First decide which sides you have and want: opposite, adjacent, or hypotenuse. Then pick sine, cosine, or tangent so those two sides appear in the formula, plug in your known values, and solve. For example, if a ramp rises at a known angle and you know how long the ramp is, sine of that angle times the ramp length gives the height it reaches.

You form the ratio of the sides you know, then ask the inverse function which angle produces that ratio. Imagine a wheelchair ramp that rises one foot over twelve feet of length: the tangent of the slope angle is one over twelve, so arctangent of that fraction tells you the ramp's angle is gentle, just under five degrees.

A radian instead measures the angle by how far you'd walk along the rim of a circle compared to its radius, so a full turn equals two pi radians, a little over six. tutorials.title: The Pythagorean Identity
tutorials.body: The Pythagorean identity says that for any angle, sine squared plus cosine squared always equals one. It comes straight from the unit circle: the point on the rim is always a distance of one from the center, and the Pythagorean theorem on its sideways and up-down legs forces those squares to add to one. Picture a person walking a circular track of radius one; no matter where they stand, their east-west distance squared plus their north-south distance squared brings them back to that fixed radius. This single rule lets you find sine if you know cosine, or vice versa.

tutorials.body: The angle of elevation is how far you tilt your gaze upward from straight-ahead level to look at something higher, like the top of a flagpole. The angle of depression is the opposite: how far you tilt downward to look at something below you, like a boat seen from a cliff. These angles are the everyday gateway to trig, because pairing the angle with one known distance lets sine, cosine, or tangent reveal a height or distance you can't reach. A lifeguard in a tall chair uses the angle of depression to a swimmer plus the chair height to estimate how far out they are.

tutorials.title: The Law of Sines
tutorials.body: The law of sines extends trig to triangles that don't have a right angle. It says each side divided by the sine of the angle across from it gives the same value for all three sides. So if you know one side and its opposite angle, plus one more angle or side, you can find the rest. Surveyors use this to map a far landmark: measure the angle to it from two ends of a known baseline, and the law of sines turns those angles into the distances out to the landmark.

tutorials.title: The Law of Cosines
tutorials.body: The law of cosines is a beefed-up Pythagorean theorem that works for any triangle, not just right ones. It says one side squared equals the sum of the other two sides squared, minus a correction term that uses the cosine of the angle between them. When that angle is a square corner, the cosine is zero and the formula collapses back into plain old Pythagoras. It's the tool you reach for when you know two sides and the angle wedged between them and want the third side, like finding the straight-line distance between two trails that split apart at a known angle.

tutorials.title: Why Sine and Cosine Make Waves
tutorials.body: Sine and cosine repeat forever because they track a point going around the unit circle, and every full lap brings it back to where it started. If you plot the height of that spinning point over time, you get a smooth up-and-down curve called a wave, rising to a peak, dipping to a trough, and doing it again on a fixed cycle. This is exactly how a child on a swing moves, or how the tide rolls in and out, or how a sound vibrates the air. That endless repeating shape is why trig is the language of anything that cycles.

tutorials.title: The Mean (Average)
tutorials.body: The mean is the 'balancing point' of a set of numbers: add them all up, then divide by how many there are. It tells you the single value every item would have if you shared the total out equally. Say four friends scored 6, 8, 10, and 8 points in a game; the total is 32, and 32 divided by 4 friends is a mean of 8 points each. The mean uses every value, so one very big or very small number can pull it up or down.

tutorials.title: The Median (Middle Value)
tutorials.body: The median is the number smack in the middle once you line all your values up from smallest to largest. If there is an odd count, it is the single middle one; if there is an even count, you average the two middle numbers. Line up the ages of five cousins as 4, 7, 9, 12, 40 and the median age is 9, the one in the center. Notice that the median barely cares about that 40-year-old outlier, which is why it often describes 'typical' better than the mean.

tutorials.body: The mode is simply the value that shows up most often in your data. A set can have one mode, several modes, or no mode at all if nothing repeats. Imagine a shoe store noting the sizes it sold one morning: 7, 8, 8, 9, 8, 10. Size 8 appears three times, more than any other, so the mode is 8 — the size to keep stocked. The mode is the only average that also works for non-number data like favorite colors.

tutorials.title: The Range (Spread)
tutorials.body: The range measures how spread out your numbers are: subtract the smallest value from the largest. A big range means the values are scattered widely, while a small range means they huddle close together. If the daily high temperatures one week were 60, 64, 58, 71, and 55 degrees, the range is 71 minus 55, which is 16 degrees. The range is quick to find but only looks at the two extremes, so it ignores everything in between.

tutorials.title: The Weighted Average
tutorials.body: A weighted average lets some values count for more than others, instead of treating every number equally. You multiply each value by its 'weight' (how much it matters), add those products, then divide by the total of the weights. Think of a class grade where the final exam counts twice as much as a quiz: if you scored high on the quiz but lower on the exam, the exam's bigger weight pulls your overall grade toward the exam score. This is exactly how report-card grades, batting averages, and stock indexes are built.

tutorials.body: A data set is just a collection of related observations gathered to answer a question. Each entry is a 'data point,' and together they form the raw material that statistics works on. If you write down the number of pages you read each night for a month, that list of nightly counts is your data set. tutorials.body: Frequency is the count of how many times a particular value appears in your data. Tallying frequencies into a table makes patterns jump out and is the first step toward charts and finding the mode. Suppose you ask classmates their favorite fruit and apple comes up several times, banana a few times, and grape just once — those counts are the frequencies. The value with the highest frequency is the mode, so frequency and mode go hand in hand.

tutorials.title: Percentiles
tutorials.body: A percentile tells you what percentage of the data falls below a given value. Being in the 90th percentile means you scored higher than about 90 percent of everyone, not that you got 90 percent of the questions right. When a doctor says a child's height is in the 75th percentile, it means roughly three out of four kids the same age are shorter. Percentiles turn a single number into a ranking that shows where it stands in the whole group.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me what it means to be in the 50th percentile.

tutorials.title: Standard Deviation
tutorials.body: Standard deviation measures how far, on average, the values stray from the mean — it puts a number on the 'typical distance' from the center. A small standard deviation means the data clusters tightly around the mean; a large one means the values are spread out. Imagine two archers whose arrows both average the bullseye: one peppers arrows all over the target (big standard deviation) while the other lands them in a tight cluster (small standard deviation). It is the go-to gauge of consistency, used everywhere from test scores to weather to factory quality checks.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me how range and standard deviation are different.

triggers: how does a skewed distribution work
tutorials.title: Skewed Data
tutorials.body: Data is skewed when it leans to one side, with a long tail stretching out toward the high or low end instead of being balanced. In a right-skewed set most values sit on the low side but a few big ones drag a tail to the right, pulling the mean above the median. Household incomes in a town are a classic example: most people earn modest amounts, but a handful of very high earners stretch the tail, so the average income looks higher than what a typical family actually makes. When data is skewed, the median usually describes the 'typical' value better than the mean.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me why the median beats the mean for skewed data.

triggers: how do you find average speed
tutorials.title: Average Rate (Like Average Speed)
tutorials.body: An average rate spreads a total change evenly over the total time or distance, even if the real pace bounced around. For speed, you divide the total distance by the total time — not by averaging the individual speeds. If you drive 120 miles and it takes 3 hours, your average speed is 120 divided by 3, which is 40 miles per hour, whether you were crawling in traffic or zooming on the highway in between. The average rate answers 'overall, how fast?' without worrying about the ups and downs along the way.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the average speed for 120 miles in 3 hours'.

triggers: how do you split a log of a product
tutorials.title: The Logarithm Product Rule
tutorials.body: The product rule says the log of two numbers multiplied together equals the sum of their individual logs: log(a*b) = log(a) + log(b). It works because logs measure exponents, and multiplying powers means adding the exponents underneath. This is the trick that let astronomers and navigators turn slow multiplication into quick addition for centuries. For example, log(1000) can be found as log(10) + log(100), since 1000 = 10 * 100.
tutorials.tryIt: Rewrite log(6) as a sum of two simpler logs.

tutorials.title: The Logarithm Quotient Rule
tutorials.body: The quotient rule says the log of a division equals the difference of the logs: log(a/b) = log(a) - log(b). It mirrors the product rule because dividing powers means subtracting their exponents. So if you know the logs of the top and bottom of a fraction, you just subtract to get the log of the whole thing. For instance, log(100/10) equals log(100) - log(10).
tutorials.tryIt: Express log(7/3) as a difference of two logs.

tutorials.title: The Logarithm Power Rule
tutorials.body: The power rule lets you bring an exponent out in front of a log as a multiplier: log(a^n) = n * log(a). It works because raising a number to a power repeats the multiplication, which repeats the addition of the exponent. This rule is what makes logs so handy for solving equations where the unknown sits up in an exponent. For example, log(8) can be written as log(2^3) = 3 * log(2).
tutorials.tryIt: Rewrite log(5^4) using the power rule.

tutorials.title: The Natural Logarithm (ln)
tutorials.body: The natural logarithm, written ln(x), is just a logarithm whose base is the special number e (about 2.718). It answers the question 'e to what power gives x?' and shows up anywhere growth or decay happens continuously, like compound interest or cooling coffee. Because e arises naturally in calculus and the real world, ln is the 'default' log in higher math. For example, ln(e) equals one, since e to the first power is e.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me what ln(e) is and why.

triggers: log of any base on a calculator
how to compute log of any base
tutorials.title: The Change of Base Formula
tutorials.body: Most calculators only have buttons for base-10 log and natural log, but the change of base formula lets you compute a log in any base: log base b of x equals log(x) / log(b), using whichever common base you like for both. Since the same base cancels in the ratio, the answer is the same no matter which one you pick. This is how you'd find something like a base-2 log on a regular calculator. For example, log base 2 of 8 equals log(8) / log(2).
tutorials.tryIt: Show how to compute log base 2 of 16 using change of base.

tutorials.title: Logs and Exponents Are Inverses
tutorials.body: A logarithm is the inverse operation of an exponential, meaning it undoes raising to a power the way subtraction undoes addition. If b raised to the y equals x, then log base b of x equals y; the log simply hands back the exponent. This is why log base b of (b^x) gives you x, and b raised to (log base b of x) gives you back x. For example, since 2^5 = 32, the log base 2 of 32 is 5.
tutorials.tryIt: Tell me a power like 3^4 and I'll write the matching log.

triggers: take the log of both sides
solve for x in the exponent
tutorials.title: Solving Equations With x in the Exponent
tutorials.body: When the unknown is stuck up in an exponent, you take the log of both sides and use the power rule to pull the exponent down where you can solve for it. The steps are: take log of both sides, move the exponent out front, then divide. This turns an impossible-looking exponential equation into a simple division. For example, to solve 2^x = 10, take logs to get x = log(10) / log(2).
tutorials.tryIt: Give me an equation like 3^x = 20 and I'll set up the log step.

tutorials.title: What a Logarithmic Scale Is
tutorials.body: On a logarithmic scale, equal steps along the axis represent multiplying by a fixed factor rather than adding a fixed amount, so each tick might mean ten times larger. This lets you display values that span a huge range, from tiny to enormous, on a single readable chart. Scientists use it for things that grow by multiplication instead of addition. For example, on a log scale the distance from 1 to 10 is the same as the distance from 10 to 100.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me why earthquakes and sound are measured on log scales.

triggers: how loud is double the sound
tutorials.title: Decibels: Loudness on a Log Scale
tutorials.body: The decibel scale measures sound intensity using logarithms because our ears respond to enormous ranges of power, and logs compress that range into manageable numbers. On this scale, adding a fixed number of decibels corresponds to multiplying the sound power by a fixed factor, not just adding a little. That is why a small jump in decibels can mean a big jump in actual sound energy. For example, the difference between a whisper and a jet engine is only a few dozen decibels even though the power difference is gigantic.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me why 10 dB more means ten times the sound power.

tutorials.title: The pH Scale Is Logarithmic
tutorials.body: The pH scale measures how acidic or basic a liquid is using the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, which is why it runs roughly 0 to 14 instead of spanning huge raw numbers. Because it is logarithmic, each whole step on the scale means a tenfold change in acidity, not just a small change. So a drop of one pH unit means the liquid became ten times more acidic. For example, lemon juice near pH 2 is far more than twice as acidic as water near pH 7.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me how much more acidic pH 4 is than pH 6.

triggers: why earthquakes use a log scale
tutorials.title: Earthquakes and the Logarithmic Richter Scale
tutorials.body: Earthquake magnitude scales are logarithmic, so each whole-number increase in magnitude represents about ten times more ground shaking measured by a seismograph. This compresses earthquakes that range from barely detectable to catastrophic onto one tidy number line. It also explains why a seemingly small jump in magnitude is actually a massive jump in motion. For example, a magnitude 6 quake produces about ten times the amplitude of a magnitude 5 quake.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me how much bigger a magnitude 7 is than a magnitude 5.

tutorials.title: Two Logs You Should Just Know
tutorials.body: Two log values come up constantly: the log of 1 in any base is always 0, and the log of the base itself is always 1. The first is true because any base raised to the power 0 equals 1, and the second because any base raised to the power 1 is just itself. Knowing these instantly speeds up a lot of log work. For example, log base 5 of 1 is 0, and log base 5 of 5 is 1.
tutorials.tryIt: Tell me a base and I'll give you its log of 1 and log of itself.

tutorials.title: Logarithmic Growth
tutorials.body: Logarithmic growth describes a quantity that rises quickly at first and then slows down more and more, the mirror image of fast-accelerating exponential growth. Its curve keeps climbing but flattens out, because reaching the next level requires a much bigger input each time. You see it whenever early progress is easy but further gains get harder. For example, the amount of practice needed to improve a skill often grows logarithmically: the first gains come fast, then later gains take far more effort.
tutorials.tryIt: Ask me how logarithmic growth differs from exponential growth.

tutorials.title: Adding and Subtracting Mod n
tutorials.body: To add or subtract mod n, you do the normal operation and then take the remainder mod n. The handy part is that you can reduce the inputs first or the answer at the end and get the same result. For example, mod 12, the time 9 + 7 = 16, and 16 mod 12 = 4, so 7 hours after 9 o'clock is 4 o'clock. Subtraction wraps the same way: 2 - 5 mod 12 = -3 mod 12 = 9.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is (9 + 7) mod 12'.

tutorials.title: Multiplying Mod n
tutorials.body: Multiplication mod n works like ordinary multiplication, except you keep only the remainder after dividing by n. A useful shortcut is that you may reduce each factor mod n before multiplying, which keeps the numbers small. For example, mod 7, the product 4 times 5 is 20, and 20 mod 7 = 6. This is the workhorse behind hashing and cryptography, where the same operation runs on huge numbers.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is (4 × 5) mod 7'.

triggers: raise to a power mod n
how to compute powers mod n
tutorials.title: Modular Exponentiation
tutorials.body: Modular exponentiation finds a number raised to a power, then takes the remainder mod n, without ever computing the giant power directly. The trick is to reduce mod n after each multiplication, and to square repeatedly so you reach big exponents in only a handful of steps. For example, mod 5, three squared is 9, and 9 mod 5 = 4. This is what lets RSA encryption raise numbers to enormous exponents quickly.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is (3^2) mod 5'.

triggers: how to find the inverse mod n
tutorials.title: Modular Inverse
tutorials.body: The modular inverse of a number a mod n is the number that multiplies with a to give a remainder of 1. It plays the role that dividing plays in ordinary math, since there is no direct division in modular arithmetic. An inverse exists only when a and n share no common factor other than 1. For example, mod 7, the inverse of 3 is 5, because 3 times 5 is 15, and 15 mod 7 = 1.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the inverse of 3 mod 7'.

triggers: a is congruent to b mod n
what does congruent mod n mean
tutorials.title: Congruence Mod n
tutorials.body: Two numbers are congruent mod n when they leave the same remainder after dividing by n, which is the same as saying their difference is a multiple of n. We write this with a special three-line equals sign, but the everyday meaning is that the two numbers land on the same spot when you wrap around the cycle. For instance, 17 and 5 are congruent mod 12 because both point to the 5 on a clock face. Congruence sorts every whole number into one of n groups by remainder.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'are 17 and 5 congruent mod 12'.

tutorials.title: Residue Classes
tutorials.body: A residue class mod n is the whole set of numbers that share one particular remainder when divided by n. There are exactly n of these classes, usually labeled by the remainders from 0 up to n minus 1. Mod 3, for example, every integer falls into the class of remainder 0, remainder 1, or remainder 2, so numbers like 2, 5, 8, and 11 all belong to the same class. Doing arithmetic mod n really means doing arithmetic on these classes rather than on individual numbers.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'which residue class is 11 in mod 3'.

triggers: what is the chinese remainder theorem
tutorials.title: The Chinese Remainder Theorem
tutorials.body: The Chinese Remainder Theorem says that if you know a number's remainders for several moduli that share no common factors, there is exactly one matching value within their product. It lets you stitch separate remainder clues back into a single answer. A classic riddle asks for a number leaving remainder 2 when divided by 3 and remainder 3 when divided by 5; the value 8 fits both. Computers use it to break one huge calculation into smaller independent ones run in parallel.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'find a number that is 2 mod 3 and 3 mod 5'.

tutorials.title: Euler's Theorem
tutorials.body: Euler's theorem says that if a number a shares no common factor with n, then a raised to the totient of n leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by n. The totient counts how many numbers below n are coprime to it, and this generalizes Fermat's little theorem to moduli that are not prime. For example, the totient of 10 is 4, and 3 raised to the 4th power is 81, which leaves remainder 1 mod 10. This is the property that makes RSA decryption undo encryption.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the totient of 10'.

triggers: what does phi of n mean
tutorials.title: Euler's Totient Function
tutorials.body: Euler's totient of n counts how many whole numbers from 1 up to n share no common factor with n other than 1. For a prime p the answer is simply p minus 1, because every smaller number is coprime to a prime. For 12, the coprime numbers are 1, 5, 7, and 11, so the totient of 12 is 4. This count appears anywhere you need to know how many invertible elements exist mod n.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the totient of 12'.

tutorials.title: Quadratic Residues
tutorials.body: A quadratic residue mod n is any remainder you can get by squaring a number and reducing mod n. Not every remainder is reachable this way, which is why some numbers have a square root mod n and others do not. Mod 5, squaring 1, 2, 3, and 4 gives remainders 1, 4, 4, and 1, so 1 and 4 are residues while 2 and 3 are non-residues. This split matters in cryptography and in tests for whether a number is a perfect square.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'is 4 a quadratic residue mod 5'.

tutorials.title: Primitive Roots
tutorials.body: A primitive root mod n is a number whose powers cycle through every nonzero remainder before repeating. It acts like a generator that can reach the whole group of invertible remainders one step at a time. Mod 7, the number 3 is a primitive root because its powers run through 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, and 1, hitting all six nonzero remainders. Primitive roots underpin Diffie-Hellman key exchange, where the cycling makes the secret hard to reverse.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'is 3 a primitive root mod 7'.

tutorials.title: The Discrete Logarithm
tutorials.body: The discrete logarithm asks which exponent you must raise a base to, mod n, in order to land on a given target remainder. It is the modular cousin of the ordinary logarithm, but with a wrapping number line instead of a smooth one. Mod 7, raising 3 to the power 4 gives 81, which is 4 mod 7, so the discrete log of 4 to base 3 is 4. Finding it is believed to be very hard for large n, and that difficulty is the lock behind several encryption schemes.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what power of 3 gives 4 mod 7'.

triggers: how do divisibility rules use modular arithmetic
why does the digit sum rule work
tutorials.title: Divisibility Rules and Mod
tutorials.body: The familiar divisibility shortcuts are really statements in modular arithmetic. Because 10 leaves remainder 1 mod 9, every power of 10 also leaves remainder 1, so a number and its digit sum are congruent mod 9; that is why adding the digits tests divisibility by 9. The same idea, called casting out nines, lets you spot arithmetic mistakes by checking remainders. For 1234, the digits add to 10, which is 1 mod 9, so 1234 also leaves remainder 1 when divided by 9.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the digit sum of 1234 mod 9'.

tutorials.title: Stars and Bars
tutorials.body: Stars and bars counts how many ways to distribute identical items into distinct groups. To split n identical items among k groups, you imagine n stars in a row and slide in k-1 dividers (bars); each arrangement of stars and bars is one way. The count is the number of ways to choose where the bars go among the n + k - 1 total positions, written C(n + k - 1, k - 1). For example, handing out 7 identical candies to 3 kids (allowing zero) is C(7 + 3 - 1, 3 - 1) = C(9, 2) ways.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me how many ways to give 5 identical coins to 3 people.

tutorials.title: Circular Permutations
tutorials.body: When you arrange objects in a circle, rotations that look the same shouldn't be counted twice, so there are fewer arrangements than in a straight line. For n people around a round table, fix one person's seat as a reference and arrange the rest, giving (n - 1)! distinct arrangements instead of n!. For example, 4 friends around a table can be seated in (4 - 1)! = 3! = 6 ways. If the circle can also be flipped over (like beads on a necklace), you divide by 2 more because a mirror image counts as the same.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask how many ways 5 people can sit around a round table.

tutorials.title: Arranging Items With Repeats
tutorials.body: When some items are identical, swapping two copies doesn't make a new arrangement, so you must divide out the duplicates. To arrange n items where one value repeats a times, another b times, and so on, the count is n! divided by (a! times b! times ...). For example, the word LEVEL has 5 letters with L twice and E twice, so it has 5! / (2! times 2!) = 120 / 4 = 30 distinct arrangements. This is why a word with all different letters has more anagrams than one with repeats.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask how many ways to arrange the letters in BANANA.

tutorials.title: The Pigeonhole Principle
tutorials.body: The pigeonhole principle says that if you put more items into fewer categories than there are items, at least one category must hold two or more items. More generally, if you place n items into k boxes, some box ends up with at least the ceiling of n divided by k items. For example, in any group of 13 people at least two share a birth month, because there are only 12 months. It feels obvious, but it proves surprising facts, like the certainty that two people in a large city have the exact same number of hairs.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask why any 5 socks of 2 colors guarantee a matching pair.

triggers: how many in at least one
tutorials.title: Inclusion-Exclusion
tutorials.body: Inclusion-exclusion counts items in overlapping groups without double-counting the overlaps. For two sets you add their sizes and subtract the overlap: |A or B| = |A| + |B| - |A and B|. For three sets you add the singles, subtract every pair overlap, then add back the triple overlap. For example, if 30 students take art, 25 take music, and 10 take both, the number taking at least one is 30 + 25 - 10 = 45, not 55.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask how many numbers from 1 to 20 are divisible by 2 or 3.

tutorials.title: Derangements
tutorials.body: A derangement is an arrangement where no item ends up in its original position. The classic story is a hat-check that returns hats randomly: how many ways can everyone get the wrong hat? The count of derangements of n items, written !n, can be found from a formula or built up step by step, and remarkably the fraction of permutations that are derangements settles near 1 over e (about 37 percent) as n grows. For example, the 3 derangements of 1,2,3 are 2-3-1, 3-1-2, and... checking each spot differs from its label gives exactly 2 valid ones for n = 3.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask how many ways 4 people can all get the wrong gift.

tutorials.title: Catalan Numbers
tutorials.body: Catalan numbers count many things that involve nesting or matching without crossing, like valid arrangements of parentheses. The nth Catalan number equals C(2n, n) divided by (n + 1), giving the sequence 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42 and onward. For example, there are 5 ways to fully parenthesize a product of 4 factors, and 5 distinct shapes of a binary tree with 3 internal nodes. The same number counts paths that stay above a diagonal and ways to cut a polygon into triangles, which is why mathematicians find it everywhere.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask how many ways to match 3 pairs of parentheses correctly.

triggers: expand a plus b to the n
expand a power of a binomial
tutorials.title: The Binomial Theorem
tutorials.body: The binomial theorem expands a power of a sum, (a + b)^n, into a tidy sum of terms. Each term looks like C(n, k) times a^(n-k) times b^k, and the coefficients C(n, k) are exactly the entries in Pascal's triangle. The combinatorics reason is that expanding the product means choosing b from k of the n factors, and there are C(n, k) ways to choose them. For example, (a + b)^3 = a^3 + 3a^2 b + 3ab^2 + b^3, where 1, 3, 3, 1 is row 3 of Pascal's triangle.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me to expand (x + 2) to the 3rd power.

triggers: where pascals triangle numbers come from
where do the numbers in pascals triangle come from
tutorials.title: Pascal's Triangle
tutorials.body: Pascal's triangle is a triangle of numbers where each entry is the sum of the two numbers directly above it, with 1s down both edges. Row n (counting from 0) holds the combination values C(n, 0) through C(n, n), so the triangle is a lookup table for how many ways to choose k things from n. For example, row 4 reads 1, 4, 6, 4, 1, telling you C(4, 2) = 6 ways to choose 2 items from 4. The addition rule that builds it mirrors a real choice: an item is either in your group or not, splitting each count into the two above it.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me what's in row 5 of Pascal's triangle.

triggers: number of total combinations of options
tutorials.title: The Multiplication Principle
tutorials.body: The multiplication principle says that if one choice can be made in m ways and a second independent choice in n ways, the two together can be made in m times n ways, and this extends to any number of stages. It is the engine behind almost every counting formula. For example, a menu with 3 mains, 4 sides, and 2 drinks offers 3 times 4 times 2 = 24 different meals. The key condition is that each later choice has the same number of options no matter what you picked earlier.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask how many 4-digit PIN codes are possible.

triggers: sum of a diagonal in pascals triangle
tutorials.title: The Hockey Stick Identity
tutorials.body: The hockey stick identity says that summing a diagonal of combination values in Pascal's triangle gives the single value just below and to the side, so the sum bends like a hockey stick. In symbols, C(r, r) + C(r+1, r) + ... + C(n, r) = C(n+1, r+1). For example, C(2, 2) + C(3, 2) + C(4, 2) = 1 + 3 + 6 = 10, which equals C(5, 3) = 10. It is handy for collapsing a long sum of choose-values into one term.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me to add C(1,1) + C(2,1) + C(3,1).

tutorials.title: Arranging k Out of n (nPr)
tutorials.body: A k-permutation is an ordered selection of k items chosen from n, written P(n, k) or nPr. Because order matters and items aren't reused, you multiply the shrinking pool: n choices for the first slot, n-1 for the second, down through k factors, which equals n! divided by (n - k)!. For example, awarding gold, silver, and bronze to 8 runners gives P(8, 3) = 8 times 7 times 6 = 336 outcomes. Dividing a k-permutation count by k! removes the ordering and turns it into a combination.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask how many ways to pick a 1st and 2nd place from 6 teams.

triggers: count by matching one to one
tutorials.title: Counting by Bijection
tutorials.body: A bijection is a perfect one-to-one matching between two sets, and if such a matching exists the sets must have exactly the same size. Combinatorialists use this to count a hard-to-count set by pairing each of its items with an item in an easier set. For example, the number of subsets of a 3-element set equals the number of length-3 strings of yes/no, because each subset matches the string saying whether each element is included, giving 2 times 2 times 2 = 8. A related trick, double counting, finds the size of one set by counting the same collection two different ways and setting the answers equal.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me how many subsets a 4-element set has.

tutorials.title: One-Sided Limits
tutorials.body: A one-sided limit asks what value a function approaches as you slide toward a point from only one direction: the left-hand limit comes from smaller x-values, the right-hand limit from larger ones. The two-sided limit exists only when the left and right limits agree. Think of walking toward a doorway from inside the room versus from the hallway: if you'd arrive at the same spot either way, the overall limit exists; if not, it doesn't.
tutorials.tryIt: Picture a step in a staircase: approaching the edge from the lower step and the upper step gives two different heights, so the limit there does not exist.

tutorials.title: Limit Laws
tutorials.body: Limit laws let you break a complicated limit into easier pieces: the limit of a sum is the sum of the limits, the limit of a product is the product of the limits, and the limit of a constant times a function is that constant times the limit. They only apply when each individual limit actually exists. It's like splitting a grocery bill into separate items, totaling each, then adding them up rather than wrestling with the whole receipt at once.
tutorials.tryIt: If you know two functions' limits separately, multiply them to get the limit of their product.

triggers: find a limit by plugging in
how to evaluate limits by substitution
tutorials.title: Evaluating Limits by Direct Substitution
tutorials.body: For many friendly functions, you can find a limit just by plugging the target x-value straight into the formula. This works whenever the function is continuous there, meaning it has no break, jump, or hole at that point. Polynomials always allow this, and most everyday functions do too away from trouble spots. It's like reading a thermometer right at noon because the temperature changes smoothly with no sudden jumps.
tutorials.tryIt: For a polynomial, substitute the x-value directly and that answer is the limit.

tutorials.title: Indeterminate Forms
tutorials.body: An indeterminate form shows up when direct substitution gives an expression like zero divided by zero or infinity minus infinity, which doesn't tell you the answer by itself. The form is 'indeterminate' because the true limit could turn out to be anything depending on how the pieces shrink or grow. You have to do more work, such as factoring or simplifying, to reveal it. It's like being told two runners are 'tied' without knowing whether both are sprinting or both are crawling.
tutorials.tryIt: If plugging in gives zero over zero, don't conclude the limit is one or undefined; simplify first.

triggers: how to find limits by factoring
tutorials.title: Finding Limits by Factoring
tutorials.body: When substitution gives zero over zero, try factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling a shared factor. The cancellation removes the troublesome term that was forcing the zero in the bottom, leaving a simpler expression you can then plug into. The original function had a hole at that point, but the limit still exists because the function gets arbitrarily close to that value nearby. It's like untangling a knot in a string before measuring the length you actually care about.
tutorials.tryIt: Factor top and bottom, cancel the matching factor, then substitute into what remains.

triggers: how to find limits by rationalizing
tutorials.title: Finding Limits by Rationalizing
tutorials.body: When a limit involves a square root and substitution gives zero over zero, multiply the top and bottom by the conjugate, which is the same expression with the opposite sign in the middle. Multiplying by the conjugate turns the difference of roots into a difference of squares, clearing the root and exposing a factor you can cancel. After simplifying, substitute the value as usual. It's like rationalizing to clear a stubborn radical out of a fraction before you can work with it.
tutorials.tryIt: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate to clear the root, then simplify and substitute.

triggers: limit as x goes to infinity
limit of a rational function at infinity
tutorials.title: Limits at Infinity
tutorials.body: A limit at infinity asks what value a function settles toward as x grows without bound in the positive or negative direction, describing the function's long-run end behavior. For a rational function, compare the degrees of top and bottom: the limit follows whichever part grows faster, often approaching a horizontal asymptote. A common trick is dividing every term by the highest power of x so most terms shrink toward zero. It's like asking what your average speed approaches over a road trip that never ends.
tutorials.tryIt: For a rational function, divide every term by the highest power of x and see what survives as x grows.

tutorials.title: Horizontal Asymptotes and Limits
tutorials.body: A horizontal asymptote is a horizontal line that a graph hugs as x heads toward positive or negative infinity, and it is defined precisely by the function's limits at infinity. If the limit as x grows large equals some fixed value, the line at that height is a horizontal asymptote. A function can approach the same asymptote on both ends or different ones on each side. Think of a cooling cup of coffee leveling off toward room temperature but never quite reaching it.
tutorials.tryIt: Take the limit as x goes to infinity; if it lands on a fixed number, that number is a horizontal asymptote.

tutorials.title: Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes
tutorials.body: An infinite limit happens when a function grows without bound as x approaches a certain value, usually because the denominator shrinks toward zero while the numerator does not. We say the limit is positive or negative infinity to describe the runaway behavior, even though no actual number is reached. These points produce vertical asymptotes, where the graph shoots up or down along a vertical line. It's like the screech of feedback as a microphone gets closer and closer to its speaker.
tutorials.tryIt: If the bottom of a fraction heads to zero but the top doesn't, expect an infinite limit and a vertical asymptote.

tutorials.title: The Squeeze Theorem
tutorials.body: The squeeze theorem says that if a function is trapped between two other functions that both approach the same limit at a point, then the squeezed function must approach that limit too. It's handy when a function wiggles too wildly to evaluate directly but can be bounded above and below by tamer functions. Because the upper and lower bounds meet, there's nowhere else for the trapped function to go. It's like a younger sibling walking between two parents who arrive at the same door, so the child must arrive there as well.
tutorials.tryIt: Bound a tricky function between two functions sharing a limit; the trapped function shares that limit too.

tutorials.title: Continuity Defined by Limits
tutorials.body: A function is continuous at a point when three things all hold: the function is defined there, the limit exists there, and that limit equals the function's actual value. In plain terms, the curve has no hole, jump, or break at that spot, so you could trace it without lifting your pencil. If any of the three conditions fails, the function is discontinuous there. It's like a smoothly paved road versus one with a missing slab you'd have to hop over.
tutorials.tryIt: Check that the limit at a point exists and matches the function's value there to confirm continuity.

tutorials.title: Removable Discontinuities
tutorials.body: A removable discontinuity is a single missing point, a hole, where the limit exists but the function is either undefined there or defined to the wrong value. Because the limit exists, you could 'remove' the gap simply by redefining the function at that one point to match the limit. These often appear after a factor cancels in a fraction. It's like a knitted scarf with one dropped stitch: the pattern clearly tells you what belongs there, so the fix is a single point.
tutorials.tryIt: If a limit exists but the function has a hole there, redefining that one point removes the discontinuity.

tutorials.title: The Epsilon-Delta Idea
tutorials.body: The epsilon-delta definition makes 'approaching' precise: a limit equals L if, for every tiny tolerance epsilon you demand around L, there is a small distance delta around the target x so that staying within delta keeps the output within epsilon of L. In short, no matter how strict the output target, you can always find a tight enough input window to meet it. The challenger names a tolerance and you must respond with a matching closeness. It's like promising a thermostat can hold the room within any tightness someone asks, as long as they let you set the dial close enough.

tutorials.title: Implicit Differentiation
tutorials.body: Implicit differentiation finds a derivative when y is tangled up with x and you cannot easily solve for y by itself, like a circle equation x^2 + y^2 = r^2. The trick is to differentiate both sides with respect to x while treating y as a hidden function of x, so every time you differentiate a y term you tack on a dy/dx by the chain rule. Then you collect all the dy/dx pieces on one side and solve for dy/dx algebraically. It is like knowing how fast a balloon's height changes even though height and width are baked into one stretched-shape equation rather than written as height equals something.

tutorials.title: Second Derivative (Concavity and Acceleration)
tutorials.body: The second derivative is just the derivative of the derivative: you differentiate once to get the rate of change, then differentiate that result again. It measures how the rate itself is changing, so a positive second derivative means the curve bends upward like a smile and a negative one means it bends downward like a frown. In a moving car, the first derivative of position is speed and the second derivative is acceleration, telling you whether your speed is rising or falling. So when your foot presses the gas harder, the second derivative is positive even before you reach top speed.

tutorials.title: Critical Points
tutorials.body: A critical point is an input where the derivative is either zero or undefined, and these are the spots where a function can switch from rising to falling or the other way around. Because the derivative is the slope, a slope of zero means the curve has momentarily flattened out, which is exactly what happens at the top of a hill or the bottom of a valley. To hunt for the highest or lowest value of a function, you first solve where the derivative equals zero to get your candidate locations. Think of tossing a ball: at the instant it reaches its peak height, its upward speed is zero, and that peak is the critical point.

tutorials.title: First Derivative Test
tutorials.body: The first derivative test decides whether a critical point is a local maximum, a local minimum, or neither by checking the sign of the derivative just before and just after that point. If the derivative is positive then negative, the function rose and then fell, so you sat at a peak; if it goes negative then positive, you bottomed out in a valley. If the sign does not flip, the point is just a flat pause, not a true high or low. It is like walking a trail: if the ground tilts up then tilts down, the spot in between was a summit.

tutorials.title: Second Derivative Test
tutorials.body: The second derivative test offers a shortcut for classifying a critical point where the first derivative is zero: just plug that point into the second derivative. If the second derivative is positive the curve is bending upward like a bowl, so you have a local minimum, and if it is negative the curve bends downward like a dome, giving a local maximum. When the second derivative is zero the test is inconclusive and you fall back on the first derivative test. Picture a marble: it settles in a bowl-shaped dip (positive concavity, a minimum) but rolls off a dome-shaped bump (negative concavity, a maximum).

tutorials.title: Inflection Points
tutorials.body: An inflection point is where a curve changes its concavity, switching from bending upward to bending downward or the reverse, which shows up as the second derivative changing sign. It is not about the curve being highest or lowest, but about the moment its bend reverses direction. You find candidates by setting the second derivative to zero and then confirming the sign actually flips on either side. Think of an S-shaped slide: there is a point in the middle where it stops curving one way and starts curving the other, and that turning of the bend is the inflection point.

tutorials.title: Related Rates
tutorials.body: Related rates problems link two or more quantities through an equation and ask how fast one changes given how fast another changes. You differentiate the connecting equation with respect to time, which pulls in a rate (a per-second term) for every changing variable, then plug in the known rate to solve for the unknown one. The key insight is that the chain rule ties each variable's change to the clock. A classic example is a ladder sliding down a wall: because the ladder length is fixed, knowing how fast the foot slides outward lets you compute how fast the top slides down.

tutorials.title: Partial Derivatives
tutorials.body: A partial derivative measures how a function of several variables changes when you nudge just one input while holding all the others frozen. You differentiate normally with respect to the chosen variable and treat every other variable as if it were a fixed constant. This lets you isolate the influence of a single ingredient in a recipe with many. Imagine the temperature in a room depending on both your distance from the heater and the time of day: the partial derivative with respect to distance tells you how temperature changes as you step closer, pretending the clock has stopped.

For 12 / 2 x 3, you do 12 / 2 = 6 first, then 6 x 3 = 18. Doing 2 x 3 first would give the wrong answer, so the left-to-right rule keeps things consistent.

tutorials.body: Addition and subtraction are inverse operations — they undo each other. If 8 + 5 = 13, then 13 - 5 = 8 and 13 - 8 = 5. This is why you can check a subtraction by adding back: to test 20 - 7 = 13, add 13 + 7 and see if you get 20. You do, so it's correct.

tutorials.title: Division Undoes Multiplication
tutorials.body: Division and multiplication are inverse operations. If 6 x 7 = 42, then 42 / 7 = 6 and 42 / 6 = 7. So you can check a division by multiplying back: to test 56 / 8 = 7, compute 7 x 8 and see if it returns 56. It does, so the answer is right. Knowing your times tables makes division much easier.

tutorials.body: A remainder is what's left over when something can't be split evenly. Sharing 17 cookies among 5 friends gives each friend 3 cookies (5 x 3 = 15), with 2 cookies left over. So 17 / 5 = 3 remainder 2. The remainder is always smaller than the number you're dividing by, or you could give out more.

This trick is useful when you want decimals to have the same number of places so you can line them up and compare or add.

For 6.4 / 0.8, move both points one place right to get 64 / 8 = 8. This works because you're really multiplying top and bottom by the same power of ten, which keeps the answer the same.

tutorials.body: A remainder can be written as a fraction by putting it over the number you divided by. For 13 / 4 = 3 remainder 1, the remainder 1 over the divisor 4 gives 3 and 1/4. This makes sense when the leftover can be shared, like 13 cookies among 4 kids: each gets 3 whole cookies plus 1/4 of the last one. It turns a remainder into an exact mixed number.

For 2/9 x 3/4: the 2 and 4 share a factor of 2 (becoming 1 and 2), and the 3 and 9 share 3 (becoming 1 and 3), leaving 1/3 x 1/2 = 1/6. Canceling early means no big reducing at the end — you simplify the same total, just sooner.

For 48 / 12, both divide by 12... but try a friendlier split: divide both by 4 to get 12 / 3 = 4. For 60 / 15, divide both by 5 to get 12 / 3 = 4. tutorials.body: Angles are sorted by how open they are, measured in degrees. Acute is less than 90 degrees (sharp, like a slice of pizza). A right angle is exactly 90 degrees (a perfect corner). Obtuse is between 90 and 180 degrees (wide open). A straight angle is exactly 180 degrees (a flat line). A reflex angle is more than 180 but less than 360 degrees (it bends the long way around).

tutorials.title: Complementary Angles
tutorials.body:
Two angles are complementary when they add up to exactly 90 degrees. They fit together to make a right angle (a square corner). To find the complement of an angle, subtract it from 90.

Example: the complement of a 30 degree angle is 90 - 30 = 60 degrees. So 30 and 60 are complementary.

tutorials.title: Supplementary Angles
tutorials.body:
Two angles are supplementary when they add up to exactly 180 degrees. Together they form a straight line. To find the supplement of an angle, subtract it from 180.

Example: the supplement of a 110 degree angle is 180 - 110 = 70 degrees. So 110 and 70 are supplementary.
tutorials.example: 125 degrees and 55 degrees are supplementary because they sum to 180

tutorials.title: Vertical Angles
tutorials.body:
When two straight lines cross, they make an X shape with four angles. The angles that are directly across from each other (the opposite pairs) are called vertical angles, and they are always equal.

Example: if two lines cross and one angle is 70 degrees, the angle straight across from it is also 70 degrees. The other two angles are each 110 degrees.

All the angles sitting on one side of a straight line add up to 180 degrees. So if you know all but one of them, you can find the missing angle by subtracting from 180.

Example: two angles share a point on a line and one is 130 degrees. The other must be 180 - 130 = 50 degrees.

If several angles meet at a single point and go all the way around, they add up to 360 degrees (a full turn). Find a missing angle by subtracting the known ones from 360.

Example: three angles meet at a point: 120, 90, and one unknown. The unknown is 360 - 120 - 90 = 150 degrees.

tutorials.body:
The three inside angles of any triangle always add up to 180 degrees, no matter the shape. So if you know two angles, subtract their sum from 180 to find the third.

Example: a triangle has angles of 50 and 60 degrees. The third is 180 - 50 - 60 = 70 degrees.

tutorials.body:
The four inside angles of any four-sided shape (quadrilateral) add up to 360 degrees. That is because you can split any quadrilateral into two triangles, and 180 + 180 = 360.

Example: three angles of a quadrilateral are 90, 90, and 100. The fourth is 360 - 90 - 90 - 100 = 80 degrees.

tutorials.title: Interior Angle Sum of a Polygon
tutorials.body:
For a polygon with n sides, the inside angles add up to (n - 2) times 180 degrees. The idea: you can cut any polygon into (n - 2) triangles, and each triangle holds 180 degrees.

Example: a pentagon has 5 sides, so the sum is (5 - 2) x 180 = 3 x 180 = 540 degrees.

tutorials.body:
An exterior angle is made by extending one side of a polygon. For any convex polygon, all the exterior angles together add up to 360 degrees, no matter how many sides it has. Imagine walking around the outside and turning at each corner: you turn a full circle in total.

Example: a regular pentagon has 5 equal exterior angles, so each one is 360 / 5 = 72 degrees.

A regular polygon has all sides and all angles equal. To find one interior angle, first find the total angle sum, (n - 2) x 180, then divide by the number of angles, n.

Example: a regular hexagon has 6 sides. Sum = (6 - 2) x 180 = 720. Each angle = 720 / 6 = 120 degrees.

For three lengths to form a triangle, the two shorter sides added together must be longer than the longest side. If they are equal or shorter, the sides just lie flat and no triangle closes up.

Example: 3, 4, 5 works because 3 + 4 = 7 is greater than 5. But 2, 3, 6 fails because 2 + 3 = 5 is less than 6.

tutorials.title: What Is Perimeter
tutorials.body:
Perimeter is the total distance all the way around the edge of a flat shape. To find it, add up the lengths of every side. Think of walking around the outside of a yard: the perimeter is how far you walked.

Example: a rectangle 5 cm by 3 cm has perimeter 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm.

Area is the amount of flat space inside a shape, measured in square units (like square centimeters). Imagine covering the shape with little squares and counting them. Area tells you how much surface something covers, such as the carpet needed for a floor.

Example: a 3 by 4 grid of unit squares has 12 little squares, so the area is 12 square units.

tutorials.title: Euler's Formula for Solids
tutorials.body:
For any solid shape with flat faces (a polyhedron), the number of faces plus the number of vertices is always two more than the number of edges: Faces + Vertices = Edges + 2.

Example: a cube has 6 faces and 8 vertices. 6 + 8 = 14, and edges + 2 = 12 + 2 = 14. It matches!

Example: a cube with side 2 has 6 faces, each 2 x 2 = 4. Total surface area = 6 x 4 = 24 square units.

Example: a box 2 by 3 by 4 holds 2 x 3 x 4 = 24 little cubes, so its volume is 24 cubic units.
