tutorials.body: Length measures distance. In the metric system the units, from small to big, are millimeters (mm), centimeters (cm), meters (m), and kilometers (km). 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, and 1000 m = 1 km. To go from a big unit to a smaller one you multiply; from small to big you divide.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how many cm are in a meter?'

triggers: how do you convert metric length units
how to change cm to m
tutorials.title: Converting Metric Lengths
tutorials.body:
Because metric units jump by powers of ten, converting just moves the decimal point. To change a smaller unit to a bigger one (like cm to m) divide; to go from bigger to smaller multiply. 1 m = 100 cm, so multiply meters by 100 to get cm.

Example: 3.5 m = 3.5 x 100 = 350 cm. And 250 cm = 250 / 100 = 2.5 m.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'convert 4 meters to centimeters'

tutorials.title: Units of Mass
tutorials.body: Mass measures how much matter is in something. Common metric units are milligrams (mg), grams (g), kilograms (kg), and tonnes (t). 1000 mg = 1 g, 1000 g = 1 kg, and 1000 kg = 1 tonne. A paperclip is about 1 gram; a textbook is about 1 kilogram.
tutorials.example: a 2 kg bag of flour equals 2000 grams
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how many grams are in a kilogram?'

triggers: how do volume liquid units work
tutorials.title: Units of Capacity (Liquid Volume)
tutorials.body: Capacity measures how much liquid a container holds. Metric units are milliliters (mL) and liters (L), with 1000 mL = 1 L. A teaspoon is about 5 mL, a water bottle about 500 mL, and a big soda bottle is 2 L. One liter of water also takes up 1000 cubic centimeters of space.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how many mL are in a liter?'

tutorials.title: Units of Time
tutorials.body:
Time is measured in seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, and years. 60 seconds = 1 minute, 60 minutes = 1 hour, 24 hours = 1 day, 7 days = 1 week, and about 365 days = 1 year. To convert minutes to seconds you multiply by 60; to convert seconds to minutes you divide by 60.

Example: 3 minutes = 3 x 60 = 180 seconds.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how many seconds are in 5 minutes?'

triggers: how do you find the perimeter of a compound shape
what is perimeter of an L shape
tutorials.title: Perimeter of Compound Shapes
tutorials.body: A compound shape is made of simpler shapes stuck together, often forming an L or T. To find its perimeter, carefully walk around the whole outside edge and add up every straight piece, including the steps. Missing side lengths can usually be found by comparing the longer sides on the opposite walls.
tutorials.example: an L-shape is just the total of all its outer edges added up
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you find the perimeter of an L shape?'

triggers: what is a scale on a map
tutorials.title: Scale Drawings
tutorials.body:
A scale drawing shows something big at a smaller size, keeping the same proportions. A scale like 1:100 means 1 unit on the drawing stands for 100 real units. To find a real length, multiply the drawing length by the scale number; to find a drawing length, divide.

Example: at scale 1:50, a wall drawn 4 cm long is really 4 x 50 = 200 cm = 2 m.
tutorials.example: scale 1:100, a 3 cm line means 300 cm in real life
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do scale drawings work?'

triggers: how do you read a map scale
what does 1 to 25000 mean on a map
tutorials.title: Map Scales
tutorials.body: A map scale tells you how distances on the map compare to real distances. A scale of 1:25000 means 1 cm on the map equals 25000 cm in real life (which is 250 m). To find a real distance, measure on the map and multiply by the scale number, then convert to a sensible unit.
tutorials.example: on a 1:50000 map, 2 cm represents 100000 cm = 1 km
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you read a map scale?'

tutorials.title: The Four Quadrants
tutorials.body: The two axes split the coordinate plane into four regions called quadrants, numbered with Roman numerals counterclockwise from the top right. Quadrant I (+, +) is top right; Quadrant II (-, +) top left; Quadrant III (-, -) bottom left; Quadrant IV (+, -) bottom right. The signs of x and y tell you which quadrant a point lies in.
tutorials.example: the point (-3, 5) is in Quadrant II
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'which quadrant is (-2, -4) in?'

triggers: how do you find the distance between two points
tutorials.title: Distance Between Two Points
tutorials.body:
To find how far apart two points are, you can use the Pythagorean theorem on the horizontal and vertical gaps. Find the difference in x and the difference in y, square each, add them, then take the square root.

Example: from (1, 2) to (4, 6): across is 3, up is 4. Distance = square root of (3x3 + 4x4) = square root of 25 = 5.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'distance from (1,1) to (4,5)?'

triggers: how do you find the midpoint
tutorials.title: Midpoint of a Line Segment
tutorials.body:
The midpoint is the exact middle of a line segment. To find it, take the average of the two x-coordinates and the average of the two y-coordinates: add the pair and divide by 2.

Example: the midpoint of (2, 4) and (6, 8) is ((2+6)/2, (4+8)/2) = (4, 6).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'midpoint of (1,3) and (5,7)?'

triggers: what are angles in parallel lines
what are corresponding and alternate angles
tutorials.title: Angles in Parallel Lines
tutorials.body: When a straight line (a transversal) crosses two parallel lines, special equal angles appear. Corresponding angles sit in the same position at each crossing and are equal (they form an F shape). Alternate angles are on opposite sides between the lines and are equal (a Z shape). Co-interior angles are between the lines on the same side and add to 180 (a C shape).
tutorials.example: alternate angles form a Z shape and are equal
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what are corresponding angles?'

triggers: what is a line of symmetry
tutorials.title: Lines of Symmetry
tutorials.body: A line of symmetry is a line you could fold a shape along so both halves match perfectly, like a mirror. A shape can have zero, one, or many lines of symmetry. A square has 4 lines of symmetry, a rectangle has 2, and a circle has infinitely many.
tutorials.example: a square has 4 lines of symmetry
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how many lines of symmetry does a rectangle have?'

tutorials.title: Rotational Symmetry
tutorials.body: A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks exactly the same when you turn it around its center, before a full 360 degree spin. The order of rotational symmetry is how many times it matches itself in one full turn. A square has order 4 because it looks the same every 90 degrees.
tutorials.example: a square has rotational symmetry of order 4
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the order of rotational symmetry of a square?'

triggers: what is a translation in geometry
how does sliding a shape work
tutorials.title: Translation (Sliding)
tutorials.body:
A translation slides a shape to a new spot without turning or flipping it. Every point moves the same distance in the same direction. We often describe it with how far to move right or left and up or down.

Example: translating the point (2, 3) by '4 right and 1 up' moves it to (6, 4). The shape stays exactly the same size and direction.
tutorials.example: sliding a shape 5 left and 2 down moves every point the same way
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a translation in geometry?'

triggers: what is a reflection in geometry
how does reflecting a shape work
tutorials.title: Reflection (Flipping)
tutorials.body:
A reflection flips a shape over a mirror line, creating a backwards copy. Each point and its reflection are the same distance from the mirror line, on opposite sides. The size and shape stay the same, but it faces the other way.

Example: reflecting the point (3, 2) over the y-axis gives (-3, 2).
tutorials.example: reflecting across the x-axis turns (4, 5) into (4, -5)
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a reflection in geometry?'

triggers: what is a rotation in geometry
how does rotating a shape work
tutorials.title: Rotation (Turning)
tutorials.body:
A rotation turns a shape around a fixed point called the center of rotation, by a certain angle and direction (clockwise or counterclockwise). The shape keeps its size and form, just spun to a new position. Common turns are 90, 180, and 270 degrees.

Example: rotating a shape 180 degrees about the origin turns the point (2, 3) into (-2, -3).
tutorials.example: a 90 degree turn moves the hands of a clock a quarter way around
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a rotation in geometry?'

triggers: what is an enlargement in geometry
tutorials.title: Enlargement (Resizing)
tutorials.body:
An enlargement makes a shape bigger or smaller while keeping the same proportions. The scale factor tells you how many times larger each length becomes. A scale factor of 2 doubles every side; a scale factor of 1/2 halves them. The shape stays the same kind, just a different size.

Example: enlarging a 3 cm by 2 cm rectangle by scale factor 3 makes it 9 cm by 6 cm.
tutorials.example: scale factor 2 turns a 4 cm side into an 8 cm side
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is an enlargement in geometry?'

tutorials.title: Congruent Shapes
tutorials.body: Two shapes are congruent if they are exactly the same size AND the same shape, even if one is flipped or turned. If you could pick one up and lay it perfectly on top of the other, they are congruent. All matching sides and angles are equal.
tutorials.example: two identical puzzle pieces are congruent even if you rotate one
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what does congruent mean?'

triggers: what does similar mean in geometry
tutorials.title: Similar Shapes
tutorials.body: Two shapes are similar if they are the same shape but different sizes, like a photo and its enlargement. Their angles are equal and their matching sides are all in the same ratio (the scale factor). Every pair of squares is similar; every pair of circles is similar.
tutorials.example: a small triangle and a 2x larger copy of it are similar
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what does similar mean in geometry?'

triggers: how does the pythagorean theorem work
tutorials.title: The Pythagorean Theorem
tutorials.body:
In a right triangle, the longest side (the hypotenuse, across from the right angle) is linked to the other two sides by a rule: the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. So a x a + b x b = c x c.

Example: legs 3 and 4 give 9 + 16 = 25, and the square root of 25 is 5, so the hypotenuse is 5.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the pythagorean theorem?'

tutorials.title: Pythagorean Triples
tutorials.body: A Pythagorean triple is a set of three whole numbers that fit the Pythagorean theorem perfectly, making a right triangle with no leftover decimals. The most famous is 3, 4, 5. Multiply any triple by a number and you get another, like 6, 8, 10. Other triples include 5, 12, 13 and 8, 15, 17.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what are Pythagorean triples?'

tutorials.title: What Is the Hypotenuse
tutorials.body: The hypotenuse is the longest side of a right triangle. It is always the side directly across from the right angle (the 90 degree corner), and it never touches the right angle itself. The other two shorter sides are called the legs.
tutorials.example: in a right triangle with sides 6, 8, 10, the hypotenuse is 10
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'which side is the hypotenuse?'

triggers: how many degrees are in a circle
why does a circle have 360 degrees
tutorials.title: Degrees in a Circle
tutorials.body: A full circle is divided into 360 degrees. A half circle (straight line) is 180 degrees, a quarter circle (right angle) is 90 degrees. The number 360 is handy because it divides evenly by so many numbers (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12 and more), making fractions of a turn easy.
tutorials.example: a quarter turn is 90 degrees, half of 360
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how many degrees are in a circle?'

triggers: how do you use a protractor
tutorials.title: Using a Protractor
tutorials.body: A protractor measures angles in degrees. Place its center hole on the angle's corner (the vertex) and line up one arm of the angle with the zero line. Then read where the other arm crosses the scale. Be careful: use the scale that starts at zero on your baseline, since a protractor has two sets of numbers.
tutorials.example: line the vertex on the center, baseline on zero, then read the degrees
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you use a protractor?'

tutorials.title: Bearings
tutorials.body:
A bearing is a way to describe direction using degrees, always measured clockwise from North and written with three digits. North is 000, East is 090, South is 180, and West is 270. A bearing of 045 points northeast.

Example: to face directly southeast, you would use a bearing of 135 degrees.
tutorials.example: a bearing of 270 degrees points due West
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what bearing points East?'

triggers: how do isosceles triangle angles work
what are the base angles of an isosceles triangle
tutorials.title: Angles in an Isosceles Triangle
tutorials.body:
An isosceles triangle has two equal sides, and the two angles at the bottom (base angles) opposite those equal sides are also equal. Since all three angles add to 180, if you know the top angle you can find each base angle: subtract from 180 and split the rest in half.

Example: top angle 40, so base angles are (180 - 40) / 2 = 70 each.
tutorials.example: top angle 100: base angles are each (180 - 100)/2 = 40
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'isosceles triangle with top angle 50, find the base angles'

triggers: what are the angles of an equilateral triangle
tutorials.title: Angles in an Equilateral Triangle
tutorials.body: An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal, which means all three angles are equal too. Since the angles must add up to 180 degrees, each one is 180 / 3 = 60 degrees.
tutorials.example: every angle in an equilateral triangle is exactly 60 degrees
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what are the angles of an equilateral triangle?'

triggers: why is a right angle 90 degrees
tutorials.title: What Is a Right Angle
tutorials.body: A right angle is an angle of exactly 90 degrees, the kind you see in the corner of a square, a book, or a window. It is a quarter of a full turn. We mark a right angle with a small square in the corner instead of a curved line.
tutorials.example: the corner of a piece of paper is a right angle
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a right angle?'

triggers: how many diagonals does a polygon have
tutorials.title: Diagonals of a Polygon
tutorials.body:
A diagonal is a straight line joining two corners of a shape that are not already connected by a side. A triangle has none. A quadrilateral has 2 diagonals. The number for an n-sided shape is n x (n - 3) / 2.

Example: a pentagon (5 sides) has 5 x (5 - 3) / 2 = 5 x 2 / 2 = 5 diagonals.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how many diagonals does a pentagon have?'

triggers: what are polygons named by sides
what is a polygon with 7 sides called
tutorials.title: Naming Polygons by Sides
tutorials.body: Polygons are named by their number of sides. 3 = triangle, 4 = quadrilateral, 5 = pentagon, 6 = hexagon, 7 = heptagon, 8 = octagon, 9 = nonagon, 10 = decagon, 12 = dodecagon. The names come from Greek number words, so 'oct' (eight) appears in octagon and octopus alike.
tutorials.example: a stop sign is an octagon (8 sides)
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a 6-sided shape called?'

triggers: what is the difference between regular and irregular polygons
tutorials.title: Regular vs Irregular Polygons
tutorials.body: A regular polygon has all sides the same length AND all angles equal, like a perfect honeycomb hexagon or a stop sign. An irregular polygon has sides or angles that are not all equal, like a random four-sided lot. Both can have the same number of sides; it is the equal-ness that makes one 'regular'.
tutorials.example: a square is a regular quadrilateral; a kite is an irregular one
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a regular polygon?'

triggers: what is the difference between concave and convex
tutorials.title: Concave vs Convex Shapes
tutorials.body: A convex shape has all its corners pushing outward, so no angle is bigger than 180 degrees and no part caves in, like a regular hexagon. A concave shape has at least one corner that points inward (a 'dent'), making one interior angle a reflex angle (more than 180). An arrow shape is concave.
tutorials.example: an arrow or a star shape is concave; a triangle is convex
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a concave shape?'

triggers: what is a point line and plane
what are the basic building blocks of geometry
tutorials.title: Points, Lines, and Planes
tutorials.body: These are the basic building blocks of geometry. A point marks an exact location and has no size, shown as a dot. A line is straight, goes on forever in both directions, and has no thickness. A plane is a perfectly flat surface that stretches forever in all directions, like an endless tabletop.
tutorials.example: a dot is a point, a stretched string is a line, a wall represents part of a plane
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a point in geometry?'

triggers: what is the difference between a ray and a segment
what is a ray and a line segment
tutorials.title: Rays and Line Segments
tutorials.body: A line segment is a straight piece with two endpoints, so it has a definite length. A ray starts at one endpoint and goes on forever in one direction, like a beam of light from a flashlight. A full line goes on forever in both directions with no endpoints.
tutorials.example: a flashlight beam is like a ray; a pencil mark with two ends is a segment
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a ray in geometry?'

triggers: how does a perpendicular bisector work
tutorials.title: Perpendicular Bisector
tutorials.body: A perpendicular bisector is a line that cuts a line segment exactly in half AND crosses it at a right angle (90 degrees). Every point on this line is the same distance from both ends of the segment, which makes it useful for finding the middle of things fairly.
tutorials.example: the line that splits a segment in half at 90 degrees is its perpendicular bisector
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a perpendicular bisector?'

triggers: how does an angle bisector work
tutorials.title: Angle Bisector
tutorials.body:
An angle bisector is a line or ray that splits an angle into two equal smaller angles. If you bisect a 60 degree angle, you get two 30 degree angles. Every point on the bisector is the same distance from both arms of the angle.

Example: bisecting a 90 degree angle creates two 45 degree angles.
tutorials.example: bisecting an 80 degree angle gives two 40 degree angles
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is an angle bisector?'

triggers: what is a chord and a tangent
tutorials.title: Chords, Tangents, and Secants
tutorials.body: Lines interact with a circle in different ways. A chord is a straight line joining two points on the circle (the diameter is the longest chord). A tangent just touches the circle at exactly one point and never goes inside. A secant cuts right through, crossing the circle at two points.
tutorials.example: a tangent touches a circle once, like a ball resting on the ground
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a chord of a circle?'

triggers: what is the angle in a semicircle
why is the angle in a semicircle 90
tutorials.title: Angle in a Semicircle
tutorials.body: There is a neat circle rule: if you draw a triangle where one side is the diameter and the opposite corner touches the edge of the circle, that corner angle is always exactly 90 degrees. This is sometimes called Thales' theorem.
tutorials.example: any triangle drawn on a diameter has a right angle at the far point
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the angle in a semicircle?'

tutorials.title: Tessellations
tutorials.body: A tessellation is a pattern of shapes that fit together with no gaps and no overlaps, covering a surface like floor tiles. Shapes tessellate when the angles meeting at each point add up to exactly 360 degrees. Squares, equilateral triangles, and regular hexagons all tessellate on their own.
tutorials.example: hexagons tessellate perfectly, which is why honeycombs use them
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a tessellation?'

tutorials.title: Why Hexagons Tessellate
tutorials.body: Each interior angle of a regular hexagon is 120 degrees. Where hexagons meet, three corners come together: 120 + 120 + 120 = 360 degrees, a full turn with no gap. That perfect fit, plus hexagons holding lots of space with little wall, is why bees build hexagonal honeycombs.
tutorials.example: three hexagon corners meet at 360 degrees with no gaps
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'why do hexagons tessellate?'

triggers: how do you find the area of a sector
what is the area of a pizza slice
tutorials.title: Area of a Sector
tutorials.body:
A sector is a pie-slice of a circle. Its area is a fraction of the whole circle's area, where the fraction is the slice's angle out of 360 degrees. So sector area = (angle / 360) x pi x radius x radius.

Example: a quarter slice (90 degrees) of a circle with radius 4 has area (90/360) x 3.14 x 16 = (1/4) x 50.24 = about 12.56 square units.
tutorials.example: a 90 degree slice is one-fourth of the circle's area
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the area of a sector?'

triggers: how do you find arc length
what is the length of an arc
tutorials.title: Length of an Arc
tutorials.body:
An arc is part of the circle's edge. Its length is a fraction of the full circumference, where the fraction is the arc's angle out of 360 degrees. So arc length = (angle / 360) x pi x diameter.

Example: a 90 degree arc on a circle with diameter 10 has length (90/360) x 3.14 x 10 = (1/4) x 31.4 = about 7.85 units.
tutorials.example: a half-circle arc (180 degrees) is half the full circumference
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you find arc length?'

triggers: how do you find the volume of a pyramid
what is the volume of a pyramid
tutorials.title: Volume of a Pyramid
tutorials.body:
A pyramid holds one-third the volume of a prism (box) with the same base and height. So its volume is (1/3) x base area x height.

Example: a pyramid with a square base 6 by 6 (area 36) and height 5 has volume (1/3) x 36 x 5 = (1/3) x 180 = 60 cubic units.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'volume of a pyramid base area 30 height 4?'

triggers: how are liters and cubic centimeters related
what is the link between capacity and volume
tutorials.title: Capacity and Volume Link
tutorials.body: Liquid capacity and cubic space are connected. 1 milliliter takes up exactly 1 cubic centimeter, and 1 liter equals 1000 cubic centimeters (which is the size of a 10 cm cube). So if you know a container's volume in cubic cm, you instantly know its capacity in mL.
tutorials.example: a box of 1000 cubic cm holds 1 liter of water
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how many cubic cm are in a liter?'

triggers: how do you read a measuring scale
how to read marks on a ruler or jug
tutorials.title: Reading Measurement Scales
tutorials.body:
To read a ruler, measuring jug, or scale, first work out what each small mark is worth by counting the gaps between two labeled numbers. If 5 gaps fill the space from 0 to 100, each gap is 100 / 5 = 20. Then count the marks to the pointer.

Example: marks every 50 mL, pointer 3 marks above 200, reads 200 + 150 = 350 mL.
tutorials.example: if 10 gaps span 0 to 50, each mark is worth 5
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you read a measuring scale?'

triggers: how do you convert area units
why is 1 square meter 10000 square cm
tutorials.title: Converting Area Units
tutorials.body:
Area units do not convert the same way as lengths, because area uses two dimensions. Since 1 m = 100 cm, a square meter is 100 cm x 100 cm = 10000 square cm, not just 100. So you square the length conversion factor when converting area.

Example: 2 square meters = 2 x 10000 = 20000 square cm.
tutorials.example: 1 square meter equals 10000 square cm, not 100
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how many square cm in a square meter?'

triggers: how do you convert volume units
why is 1 cubic meter a million cubic cm
tutorials.title: Converting Volume Units
tutorials.body:
Volume uses three dimensions, so the length conversion factor is cubed. Since 1 m = 100 cm, a cubic meter is 100 x 100 x 100 = 1,000,000 cubic cm. That is why a small mistake in unit conversion can be huge with volume.

Example: 3 cubic meters = 3 x 1,000,000 = 3,000,000 cubic cm.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how many cubic cm in a cubic meter?'

triggers: how are speed distance and time related
tutorials.title: Speed, Distance, and Time
tutorials.body:
These three are linked: speed = distance / time. Rearranged, distance = speed x time, and time = distance / speed. A handy triangle has distance on top, with speed and time below; cover the one you want to find.

Example: traveling 120 km in 2 hours gives speed = 120 / 2 = 60 km per hour.
tutorials.example: 60 km/h for 3 hours covers 60 x 3 = 180 km
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you find speed?'

triggers: how are density mass and volume related
tutorials.title: Density, Mass, and Volume
tutorials.body:
Density tells how packed something is: density = mass / volume. Rearranged, mass = density x volume, and volume = mass / density. Dense things like metal pack a lot of mass into a small space; light things like foam do not.

Example: 200 g packed into 100 cubic cm has density 200 / 100 = 2 g per cubic cm.
tutorials.example: mass 50 g in volume 25 cubic cm gives density 2 g/cubic cm
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you find density?'

tutorials.title: Clockwise and Counterclockwise
tutorials.body: Clockwise is the direction the hands of a clock turn: from 12 to 3 to 6 to 9 and back to 12. Counterclockwise (also called anticlockwise) is the opposite direction, going backwards around the clock. These words describe which way to turn or rotate.
tutorials.example: a clock's hands move clockwise; unscrewing a lid is usually counterclockwise
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what does clockwise mean?'

triggers: what is the net of a cylinder
tutorials.title: Net of a Cylinder
tutorials.body: If you unroll a cylinder (like a soup can), you get three flat pieces: two circles for the top and bottom, and one rectangle for the curved side. The rectangle's width is the same as the circle's circumference, because that side wrapped all the way around the circle.
tutorials.example: a can unrolls into two circles and one rectangle
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the net of a cylinder?'

triggers: how do you find the surface area of a cylinder
what is the surface area of a cylinder
tutorials.title: Surface Area of a Cylinder
tutorials.body:
A cylinder's surface is two circles plus the curved side. The two circles together are 2 x pi x radius x radius, and the curved part (a rolled-up rectangle) is the circumference times the height: 2 x pi x radius x height. Add them.

Example: radius 2, height 5: circles 2 x 3.14 x 4 = 25.12, side 2 x 3.14 x 2 x 5 = 62.8, total about 87.9 square units.
tutorials.example: two circle ends plus a wrapped rectangle make a cylinder's surface
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'surface area of a cylinder radius 3 height 4?'

tutorials.title: What Is a Vertex
tutorials.body: A vertex is a corner point where lines or edges meet (the plural is vertices). In a 2D shape it is where two sides meet, like the three corners of a triangle. In a 3D shape it is where edges meet, like the 8 corners of a cube. An angle's tip is also called its vertex.
tutorials.example: a triangle has 3 vertices; a cube has 8
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a vertex?'

tutorials.title: Adjacent Angles
tutorials.body: Adjacent angles are two angles that sit right next to each other, sharing a common arm (side) and the same corner (vertex), but not overlapping. They are like two slices of pizza side by side. If their outer arms form a straight line, the two adjacent angles add to 180 degrees.
tutorials.example: two angles sharing a side at the same point are adjacent
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what are adjacent angles?'

triggers: what is base and height in area
how do you find the height of a triangle
tutorials.title: Base and Height
tutorials.body: When finding the area of a triangle or parallelogram, the base is any chosen side and the height is the straight-up distance from that base to the opposite point or side, measured at a right angle (not along a slanted side). The base and its height must be perpendicular to each other.
tutorials.example: for a triangle, height is measured straight up from the base, not along a slope
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the height of a triangle in area?'

how are interior and exterior angles related
tutorials.title: Interior vs Exterior Angles
tutorials.body: At each corner of a polygon, the interior angle is inside the shape, and the exterior angle is the angle made by extending a side outward. The two sit on a straight line, so they always add up to 180 degrees. If an interior angle is 110, its exterior angle is 180 - 110 = 70.

tutorials.title: Square Numbers as Areas
tutorials.body: A square number, like 4, 9, or 16, gets its name because that many dots can be arranged into a perfect square. 3 squared is 9, which is a 3 by 3 grid of 9 dots. This is the same idea as the area of a square: side times side.
tutorials.example: 16 is a square number because 4 x 4 dots make a square

tutorials.title: Cube Numbers as Volumes
tutorials.body: A cube number, like 8, 27, or 64, is called that because you can stack that many little cubes into one big cube. 3 cubed is 27, a 3 by 3 by 3 stack. This matches the volume of a cube: side times side times side.
tutorials.example: 27 is a cube number because a 3 by 3 by 3 stack holds 27 cubes

tutorials.title: Central Angle of a Regular Polygon
tutorials.body:
If you put a dot at the center of a regular polygon and draw lines to each corner, you split it into equal triangles. Each central angle is 360 degrees divided by the number of sides.

Example: a regular pentagon (5 sides) has central angles of 360 / 5 = 72 degrees each.
tutorials.example: a regular hexagon has central angles of 360 / 6 = 60 degrees

tutorials.title: Perimeter of a Regular Polygon
tutorials.body:
A regular polygon has all sides equal, so its perimeter is just the number of sides times the length of one side: n x side.

Example: a regular pentagon with each side 6 cm has perimeter 5 x 6 = 30 cm.
tutorials.example: a regular hexagon with side 4: 6 x 4 = 24

tutorials.title: The Three Dimensions
tutorials.body: A flat shape has two dimensions: length and width (so we call it 2D). A solid object adds a third, height (or depth), making it 3D. A line is 1D (just length), a sheet of paper is roughly 2D, and a box is 3D. Each new dimension lets the object spread in a new direction.
tutorials.example: a piece of paper is 2D; a thick book is 3D

tutorials.body: Unfolding a square-based pyramid gives a flat net of one square (the base) with a triangle attached to each of its four sides, folding up to meet at the top point. A triangle-based pyramid (tetrahedron) unfolds into four triangles. Nets help you find surface area by showing every face flat.

tutorials.title: Right Angles in Shapes
tutorials.body: Some shapes are full of right angles. A rectangle and a square each have 4 right angles, one at every corner. A right-angled triangle has exactly 1. An L-shaped hexagon can have several. Spotting right angles (square corners) helps you recognize and measure shapes quickly.
tutorials.example: a rectangle has 4 right angles, one in each corner

tutorials.title: Finding a Reflex Angle
tutorials.body:
A reflex angle is more than 180 degrees. To find one, measure the smaller angle on the other side, then subtract from 360 (since the two together make a full turn).

Example: if the inside angle is 110 degrees, the reflex angle going the long way around is 360 - 110 = 250 degrees.
tutorials.example: a small angle of 70 means the reflex angle is 360 - 70 = 290

triggers: how do you find the area of a rhombus
what is the area of a rhombus
tutorials.title: Area of a Rhombus
tutorials.body:
A rhombus is a slanted square with equal sides. One easy way to find its area uses the two diagonals: multiply them and divide by 2, since the diagonals cross at right angles. So area = (diagonal1 x diagonal2) / 2.

Example: diagonals 6 and 8 give area (6 x 8) / 2 = 48 / 2 = 24 square units.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'area of a rhombus with diagonals 5 and 12?'

triggers: how do you find the area of a kite
what is the area of a kite shape
tutorials.title: Area of a Kite
tutorials.body:
A kite's diagonals cross at right angles, so just like a rhombus, its area is half the product of the two diagonals: (diagonal1 x diagonal2) / 2.

Example: a kite with diagonals 8 and 6 has area (8 x 6) / 2 = 48 / 2 = 24 square units.

tutorials.title: Most Area for a Fixed Perimeter
tutorials.body: If you have a fixed amount of fencing (perimeter), the shape that encloses the most area is a circle. Among rectangles with a fixed perimeter, a square wins. So a square garden holds more space than a long thin one using the same fence, and a circle beats them all.

tutorials.title: What Is a Polygon
tutorials.body: A polygon is a flat, closed 2D shape made only of straight sides that join end to end with no gaps. Triangles, squares, and pentagons are polygons. A shape with a curved side (like a circle) or one that does not close up is not a polygon.
tutorials.example: a hexagon is a polygon, but a circle is not (it has no straight sides)

tutorials.body: Not every arrangement of faces folds into the solid. A net is valid only if folding the faces leaves no gaps and no overlaps, and every face ends up in the right place. A cube has 11 different valid nets; many other six-square arrangements look fine flat but overlap when folded.

what are flat and solid shapes
tutorials.title: 2D vs 3D Shapes
tutorials.body: A 2D shape is flat, like a drawing on paper, with only length and width; examples are circles, squares, and triangles. A 3D shape is solid and takes up space, with length, width, and height; examples are cubes, spheres, and cones. 2D shapes have area; 3D shapes have volume and surface area.

tutorials.title: What a Coefficient Is
tutorials.body:
A coefficient is the number multiplied by a variable. In 7x, the coefficient is 7 — it tells you how many x's you have. If a variable has no number written, the coefficient is 1 (x means 1x), and -x means -1x.

Example: in 5y the coefficient is 5; in -3ab the coefficient is -3. Knowing this matters when you combine terms or factor.

triggers: how do constants work in algebra
tutorials.title: Constants in Algebra
tutorials.body:
A constant is a number on its own with no variable attached — its value never changes. In 2x + 9, the 9 is the constant. Constants combine with other constants but not with variable terms.

Example: in 3a + 4 + 7, the constants 4 and 7 add to 11, giving 3a + 11. The 3a part can't merge with them.

triggers: what is the difference expression equation
tutorials.title: Expression vs Equation
tutorials.body:
An expression is a math phrase with no equals sign — you can only simplify or evaluate it. An equation has an equals sign and claims two things are equal — you can solve it for the variable.

Example: 3x + 2 is an expression (simplify it). 3x + 2 = 11 is an equation (solve it, x = 3). The equals sign is the key difference.
tutorials.example: 4x - 1 is an expression; 4x - 1 = 7 is an equation
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'difference between expression and equation'.

tutorials.title: The Distributive Property
tutorials.body:
The distributive property says a(b + c) = ab + ac. You multiply the outside number by every term inside the parentheses. This works with subtraction too.

Example: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. With a minus: 5(2y - 3) = 10y - 15. Watch the signs: -2(x - 6) = -2x + 12 because -2 times -6 is +12.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the distributive property'.

triggers: how do you factor out the greatest common factor
what is factoring out a common factor
tutorials.title: Factoring Out the GCF
tutorials.body:
Factoring is distribution in reverse. Find the greatest common factor of all terms and pull it outside parentheses, leaving what's left inside.

Example: 6x + 9. The GCF of 6 and 9 is 3, so 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3). With variables: 4x^2 + 8x has GCF 4x, giving 4x(x + 2). Check by distributing back.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you factor out the gcf'.

triggers: how do you solve equations with parentheses
tutorials.title: Solving Equations With Parentheses
tutorials.body:
When an equation has parentheses, distribute first to clear them, then combine like terms, then solve the normal way.

Example: 3(x + 2) = 18. Distribute: 3x + 6 = 18. Subtract 6: 3x = 12. Divide: x = 4. If both sides have parentheses, distribute both before moving terms around.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you solve equations with parentheses'.

triggers: how do you solve for a variable in a formula
tutorials.title: Solving Literal Equations
tutorials.body:
A literal equation has several letters and you solve for one of them in terms of the others, using the same inverse-operation rules as numbers.

Example: solve A = lw for w. Divide both sides by l: w = A/l. For y = mx + b solved for x: subtract b (y - b = mx), then divide by m (x = (y - b)/m). The letters just stand in for numbers.
tutorials.example: d = rt solved for t is t = d/r
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you solve for a variable in a formula'.

triggers: how do and or inequalities work
tutorials.title: Compound Inequalities
tutorials.body:
A compound inequality joins two inequalities with 'and' or 'or'. 'And' means both must be true (the overlap). 'Or' means at least one is true (the combination).

Example: 1 < x < 5 means x is between 1 and 5. Solve a sandwich like 2 < x + 1 < 6 by subtracting 1 from all three parts: 1 < x < 5. An 'or' like x < 0 or x > 3 covers two separate regions.
tutorials.example: -2 <= x < 4 covers -2 up to but not 4
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a compound inequality'.

triggers: how do you solve absolute value equations
what is an absolute value equation
tutorials.title: Absolute Value Equations
tutorials.body:
Absolute value measures distance from zero, so |x| = 5 has two answers: x = 5 and x = -5. To solve, isolate the absolute value, then split into two cases (positive and negative).

Example: |x - 2| = 3. Case 1: x - 2 = 3, so x = 5. Case 2: x - 2 = -3, so x = -1. Both are solutions. If the absolute value equals a negative number, there's no solution.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you solve absolute value equations'.

tutorials.title: What a Function Is
tutorials.body:
A function is a rule that takes an input and gives exactly one output. Think of it as a machine: put in a number, get one number out. Each input maps to only one output (but different inputs can share an output).

Example: the rule 'double it' is a function: input 3 gives 6, input 5 gives 10. A rule that gave two different outputs for the same input would NOT be a function.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a function'.

triggers: what does f of x mean
tutorials.title: Function Notation f(x)
tutorials.body:
f(x) is read 'f of x' and names a function f with input x. It does NOT mean f times x. The whole f(x) stands for the output. To evaluate, plug the input into the rule.

Example: if f(x) = 2x + 1, then f(3) = 2(3) + 1 = 7. f(0) = 1. You can use other letters too, like g(x) or h(t).

triggers: how do domain and range work
tutorials.title: Domain and Range
tutorials.body:
The domain is the set of all allowed inputs (x-values). The range is the set of all possible outputs (y-values). Domain answers 'what can go in?', range answers 'what comes out?'

Example: for f(x) = x^2, the domain is all real numbers (any x works), but the range is y >= 0 because squaring never gives a negative. Watch for inputs that break things, like dividing by zero.
tutorials.example: f(x) = 1/x has domain all x except 0
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what are domain and range'.

how to tell if a graph is a function
tutorials.title: The Vertical Line Test
tutorials.body:
The vertical line test checks if a graph is a function. If any vertical line crosses the graph more than once, it's NOT a function, because that x-value would have two outputs.

Example: a straight line or a parabola passes the test (one output per input). A sideways parabola or a full circle fails — a vertical line hits it twice.
tutorials.example: a circle fails; a parabola passes
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the vertical line test'.

triggers: what is an input output table
how do you read a function table
tutorials.title: Input-Output Tables
tutorials.body:
A function table lists inputs in one column and the matching outputs in another. To find the rule, look at how each input changes into its output.

Example: inputs 1, 2, 3 give outputs 4, 5, 6 — each output is input + 3, so the rule is y = x + 3. If inputs 1, 2, 3 give 2, 4, 6, the rule is y = 2x.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is an input output table'.

tutorials.title: What Slope Means
tutorials.body:
Slope measures how steep a line is — how much y changes for each step in x. It's 'rise over run': the vertical change divided by the horizontal change. Positive slope goes up, negative goes down, zero is flat.

Example: going from (0, 1) to (2, 5), the rise is 4 and the run is 2, so slope = 4/2 = 2. The line climbs 2 units for every 1 unit right.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is slope'.

triggers: explain y equals mx plus b
how does slope intercept form work
tutorials.title: Slope-Intercept Form
tutorials.body:
Slope-intercept form is y = mx + b, where m is the slope and b is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis). It's the quickest way to graph a line: start at b, then use the slope to step.

Example: y = 2x + 3 has slope 2 and y-intercept 3. Start at (0, 3), go up 2 and right 1 to plot the next point.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is slope intercept form'.

triggers: how do you find the y intercept
tutorials.title: The Y-Intercept
tutorials.body:
The y-intercept is where a line or curve crosses the y-axis, which always happens when x = 0. In y = mx + b, the y-intercept is simply b. To find it from an equation, set x = 0 and solve for y.

Example: y = 3x - 5. Set x = 0: y = -5, so the y-intercept is (0, -5). It often represents a starting value in word problems.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the y intercept'.

triggers: how do you find the x intercept
tutorials.title: The X-Intercept
tutorials.body:
The x-intercept is where a graph crosses the x-axis, which happens when y = 0. To find it, set y to 0 and solve for x. X-intercepts are also called zeros or roots of a function.

Example: y = 2x - 6. Set y = 0: 0 = 2x - 6, so x = 3. The x-intercept is (3, 0).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the x intercept'.

triggers: what is standard form of a line
tutorials.title: Standard Form of a Line
tutorials.body:
Standard form is Ax + By = C, where A, B, and C are usually integers. It's useful for finding both intercepts quickly and for systems of equations. You can convert to slope-intercept form by solving for y.

Example: 2x + 3y = 12. Find x-intercept (y=0): x = 6. Find y-intercept (x=0): y = 4. To get slope form: y = (-2/3)x + 4.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is standard form of a line'.

triggers: how do you find slope from two points
how to calculate slope between points
tutorials.title: Slope From Two Points
tutorials.body:
With two points, slope = (change in y) / (change in x) = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1). Subtract the y's on top and the x's on bottom, keeping the order consistent.

Example: points (1, 2) and (4, 11). Slope = (11 - 2)/(4 - 1) = 9/3 = 3. The line rises 3 for every 1 across.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you find slope from two points'.

triggers: what is the slope of parallel lines
tutorials.title: Slopes of Parallel Lines
tutorials.body:
Parallel lines never meet, and the reason is they have the exact same slope. They climb at the identical rate but cross the y-axis at different spots.

Example: y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x - 4 are parallel — both have slope 2. To write a line parallel to a given one, copy its slope and use a new point to find the intercept.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the slope of parallel lines'.

triggers: what is the slope of perpendicular lines
tutorials.title: Slopes of Perpendicular Lines
tutorials.body:
Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle, and their slopes are negative reciprocals — flip the fraction and change the sign. The product of the two slopes is -1.

Example: a line with slope 2 is perpendicular to a line with slope -1/2. Slope 3/4 pairs with slope -4/3. A horizontal line (slope 0) is perpendicular to a vertical line.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the slope of perpendicular lines'.

triggers: what are horizontal and vertical lines
how do you write y = 3 or x = 2
tutorials.title: Horizontal and Vertical Lines
tutorials.body:
A horizontal line has the form y = a number; every point shares that y-value, and its slope is 0. A vertical line has the form x = a number; every point shares that x-value, and its slope is undefined.

Example: y = 4 is a flat line through all points with y = 4. x = -2 is a straight up-down line through all points with x = -2.
tutorials.example: y = 5 is horizontal; x = 3 is vertical
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what are horizontal and vertical lines'.

tutorials.title: Linear Functions
tutorials.body:
A linear function makes a straight-line graph and has a constant rate of change (constant slope). Its equation looks like f(x) = mx + b. Each step in x changes y by the same amount.

Example: f(x) = 3x + 2 adds 3 to the output every time x goes up by 1: f(0)=2, f(1)=5, f(2)=8. The equal jumps are the signature of linear.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a linear function'.

tutorials.title: Nonlinear Functions
tutorials.body:
A nonlinear function does not make a straight line — its rate of change varies. Squares, cubes, square roots, and curves are all nonlinear. In a table, the differences between outputs are not constant.

Example: f(x) = x^2 gives outputs 0, 1, 4, 9 for x = 0,1,2,3 — the jumps (1, 3, 5) keep growing, so it curves. A linear function would have equal jumps.
tutorials.example: y = x^2 curves; y = 2x is straight
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a nonlinear function'.

triggers: how does rate of change work
tutorials.title: Rate of Change
tutorials.body:
Rate of change tells how fast one quantity changes compared to another. For a line it's the slope: change in output over change in input. Real life calls it speed, cost per item, growth per year, and so on.

Example: if a plant grows from 4 cm to 10 cm over 3 days, the rate of change is (10 - 4)/3 = 2 cm per day. Same idea as slope, just with units.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is rate of change'.

tutorials.title: Composing Functions
tutorials.body:
Composing functions means feeding the output of one function into another. f(g(x)) means do g first, then put its result into f. Work from the inside out.

Example: f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x. f(g(3)): first g(3) = 6, then f(6) = 7. The order matters — g(f(3)) would give 8 instead.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is function composition'.

triggers: how do you find an inverse function
tutorials.title: Inverse Functions
tutorials.body:
An inverse function undoes what the original did. If f turns 3 into 7, its inverse turns 7 back into 3. To find it: swap x and y, then solve for y. The inverse is written f^-1(x).

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1. Write y = 2x + 1, swap: x = 2y + 1, solve: y = (x - 1)/2. So f^-1(x) = (x - 1)/2. Composing them returns the original input.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is an inverse function'.

tutorials.title: Piecewise Functions
tutorials.body:
A piecewise function uses different rules for different intervals of x. You pick which rule to use based on where the input falls.

Example: f(x) = x + 1 if x < 0, and f(x) = 2x if x >= 0. For x = -3 (negative), use the first rule: f(-3) = -2. For x = 4 (not negative), use the second: f(4) = 8. Parking fees and tax brackets work this way.
tutorials.example: f(-1) uses one rule, f(5) uses another
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a piecewise function'.

triggers: what does increasing and decreasing mean for a function
how to tell if a function is increasing
tutorials.title: Increasing and Decreasing
tutorials.body:
A function is increasing where its graph goes up as you move right (outputs grow), and decreasing where it goes down (outputs shrink). Reading left to right is key.

Example: y = x^2 decreases for x < 0 (falling toward the bottom) and increases for x > 0 (rising). A line with positive slope is increasing everywhere; negative slope is decreasing everywhere.
tutorials.example: y = -x is decreasing for all x
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what does increasing and decreasing mean for a function'.

tutorials.title: Quadratic Functions
tutorials.body:
A quadratic function has an x-squared term as its highest power: f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c. Its graph is a U-shaped curve called a parabola. If a is positive it opens up; if negative it opens down.

Example: f(x) = x^2 - 4 is a parabola opening up with its lowest point at (0, -4). The x^2 term is what makes it curve instead of going straight.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a quadratic function'.

triggers: what is the vertex of a parabola
how do you find the vertex
tutorials.title: The Vertex of a Parabola
tutorials.body:
The vertex is the turning point of a parabola — the lowest point if it opens up, or the highest if it opens down. For f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c, the vertex x-value is at x = -b/(2a), then plug in to get y.

Example: f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 5. Here a=1, b=-6, so x = 6/2 = 3. f(3) = 9 - 18 + 5 = -4. The vertex is (3, -4).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the vertex of a parabola'.

triggers: what is the axis of symmetry
how do you find the axis of symmetry
tutorials.title: Axis of Symmetry
tutorials.body:
The axis of symmetry is the vertical line that splits a parabola into two mirror-image halves. It passes through the vertex, so its equation is x = -b/(2a).

Example: f(x) = x^2 + 4x + 1 has a = 1, b = 4, so the axis is x = -4/2 = -2. Points the same distance left and right of x = -2 have equal y-values.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the axis of symmetry'.

triggers: explain vertex form of a quadratic
tutorials.title: Vertex Form of a Quadratic
tutorials.body:
Vertex form is f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k, where (h, k) is the vertex. It instantly reveals where the parabola turns and which way it opens (a's sign). Watch the sign: x - h means h is positive.

Example: f(x) = 2(x - 3)^2 + 1 has vertex (3, 1) and opens up. f(x) = -(x + 4)^2 - 2 has vertex (-4, -2) and opens down.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is vertex form'.

triggers: how do you factor a trinomial
tutorials.title: Factoring Trinomials
tutorials.body:
To factor x^2 + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. Those numbers go into two binomials.

Example: x^2 + 5x + 6. Find numbers multiplying to 6 and adding to 5: that's 2 and 3. So it factors to (x + 2)(x + 3). Check by multiplying back out. Watch signs: x^2 - x - 6 = (x - 3)(x + 2).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you factor a trinomial'.

tutorials.title: Difference of Squares
tutorials.body:
A difference of squares is a^2 - b^2, and it factors neatly into (a + b)(a - b). Spot it when you have a perfect square minus another perfect square.

Example: x^2 - 9 = (x + 3)(x - 3) because 9 is 3 squared. Also 4x^2 - 25 = (2x + 5)(2x - 5). Note: a SUM of squares (x^2 + 9) does not factor over real numbers.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is difference of squares'.

triggers: what is a perfect square trinomial
how to factor a perfect square trinomial
tutorials.title: Perfect Square Trinomials
tutorials.body:
A perfect square trinomial factors into the same binomial twice: a^2 + 2ab + b^2 = (a + b)^2, and a^2 - 2ab + b^2 = (a - b)^2. Recognize it by two perfect-square end terms and a middle term equal to 2 times their roots.

Example: x^2 + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)^2 because 3^2 = 9 and 2(3) = 6. Likewise x^2 - 10x + 25 = (x - 5)^2.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a perfect square trinomial'.

triggers: how do you complete the square
tutorials.title: Completing the Square
tutorials.body:
Completing the square turns x^2 + bx into a perfect square. Take half of b, square it, and add it. This rewrites a quadratic in vertex form or helps solve it.

Example: x^2 + 6x. Half of 6 is 3, squared is 9. So x^2 + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)^2. To solve x^2 + 6x = 7, add 9 to both sides: (x + 3)^2 = 16, so x + 3 = +-4, giving x = 1 or x = -7.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you complete the square'.

tutorials.title: The Discriminant
tutorials.body:
The discriminant is b^2 - 4ac, the part of the quadratic formula under the square root. It tells how many real solutions a quadratic has without fully solving. Positive means two solutions, zero means one, negative means none (real).

Example: x^2 + 2x + 1: discriminant = 4 - 4 = 0, so one solution. x^2 + x + 5: discriminant = 1 - 20 = -19, so no real solutions.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the discriminant'.

triggers: what is the zero product property
tutorials.title: The Zero Product Property
tutorials.body:
The zero product property says if a product equals zero, then at least one factor must be zero. This is how you solve factored quadratics: set each factor equal to zero.

Example: (x - 2)(x + 5) = 0. So either x - 2 = 0 (x = 2) or x + 5 = 0 (x = -5). The solutions are x = 2 and x = -5. It only works when one side equals zero.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the zero product property'.

triggers: what is the product rule for exponents
tutorials.title: Product Rule for Exponents
tutorials.body:
When you multiply powers with the same base, add the exponents: x^a times x^b = x^(a+b). The base stays the same — you're just counting how many factors total.

Example: x^3 times x^4 = x^7 (three x's times four x's is seven x's). With numbers: 2^2 times 2^3 = 2^5 = 32. This only works for matching bases.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the product rule for exponents'.

triggers: what is the quotient rule for exponents
tutorials.title: Quotient Rule for Exponents
tutorials.body:
When you divide powers with the same base, subtract the exponents: x^a / x^b = x^(a-b). You're cancelling matching factors top and bottom.

Example: x^7 / x^3 = x^4. With numbers: 5^6 / 5^2 = 5^4 = 625. If the bottom exponent is bigger, you'll get a negative exponent, which means a fraction.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the quotient rule for exponents'.

triggers: what is the power of a power rule
explain raising a power to a power
tutorials.title: Power of a Power
tutorials.body:
To raise a power to another power, multiply the exponents: (x^a)^b = x^(a times b). The base stays; you stack the repeated multiplication.

Example: (x^2)^3 = x^6, because x^2 used three times is x to the six. With numbers: (2^3)^2 = 2^6 = 64. Don't confuse this with the product rule, which adds.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the power of a power rule'.

triggers: what does a zero exponent mean
why is anything to the zero equal to one
tutorials.title: The Zero Exponent
tutorials.body:
Any nonzero number raised to the zero power equals 1. The reason comes from the quotient rule: x^3 / x^3 = x^0, but anything divided by itself is 1, so x^0 = 1.

Example: 7^0 = 1, (-5)^0 = 1, and (3x)^0 = 1. The only catch is 0^0, which is left undefined.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what does a zero exponent mean'.

triggers: what does a fractional exponent mean
tutorials.title: Fractional Exponents
tutorials.body:
A fractional exponent is a root. The denominator is the root, the numerator is a power: x^(1/n) is the nth root of x, and x^(m/n) is the nth root of x raised to m.

Example: 9^(1/2) = square root of 9 = 3. 8^(1/3) = cube root of 8 = 2. And 8^(2/3) = (cube root of 8)^2 = 2^2 = 4.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what does a fractional exponent mean'.

triggers: how do you simplify a radical
how to simplify a square root
tutorials.title: Simplifying Radicals
tutorials.body:
To simplify a square root, pull out perfect-square factors. Break the number into a perfect square times something else, then take the root of the perfect square.

Example: square root of 12 = square root of (4 x 3) = square root of 4 times square root of 3 = 2 times square root of 3. Square root of 50 = 5 times square root of 2.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you simplify a radical'.

triggers: how do you solve a radical equation
tutorials.title: Radical Equations
tutorials.body:
A radical equation has the variable under a square root. To solve, isolate the radical, then square both sides to remove it, then solve normally. Always check answers — squaring can create extra ones.

Example: square root of (x + 1) = 3. Square both sides: x + 1 = 9, so x = 8. Check: square root of 9 = 3. It works.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you solve a radical equation'.

triggers: how to get rid of a root in the denominator
tutorials.title: Rationalizing the Denominator
tutorials.body:
Rationalizing means clearing a square root out of the bottom of a fraction by multiplying top and bottom by that root. The fraction's value stays the same because you multiplied by a form of 1.

Example: 1/square root of 2. Multiply top and bottom by square root of 2: square root of 2 / 2. Now the denominator is a clean whole number.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is rationalizing the denominator'.

triggers: how do you solve a system by substitution
tutorials.title: Systems by Substitution
tutorials.body:
To solve a system of two equations by substitution, solve one equation for a variable, then plug that into the other equation so only one variable is left.

Example: y = x + 1 and 2x + y = 7. Substitute the first into the second: 2x + (x + 1) = 7, so 3x = 6, x = 2. Then y = 2 + 1 = 3. The solution is (2, 3).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you solve a system by substitution'.

triggers: how do you solve a system by elimination
tutorials.title: Systems by Elimination
tutorials.body:
Elimination adds or subtracts the two equations to cancel one variable. Line them up, then make one variable's coefficients opposite so they vanish when added.

Example: x + y = 10 and x - y = 4. Add them: 2x = 14, so x = 7. Plug back: 7 + y = 10, y = 3. The solution is (7, 3). Sometimes you multiply an equation first to set up the cancel.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you solve a system by elimination'.

triggers: how do you solve a system by graphing
what does the solution to a system look like on a graph
tutorials.title: Systems by Graphing
tutorials.body:
Graph both lines and the solution is the point where they cross — the (x, y) that satisfies both equations at once. Parallel lines (same slope) never cross, so there's no solution; identical lines overlap, giving infinitely many.

Example: y = x + 1 and y = -x + 5 cross at (2, 3). That single point is the system's solution.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you solve a system by graphing'.

triggers: what does no solution mean in an equation
why does an equation have no solution
tutorials.title: No Solution vs Infinite Solutions
tutorials.body:
When solving, if the variable disappears and you get a false statement (like 5 = 8), there's no solution. If you get a true statement (like 4 = 4), it's true for all values — infinitely many solutions.

Example: 2x + 3 = 2x + 7 leads to 3 = 7 (false): no solution. But 2x + 4 = 2(x + 2) gives 4 = 4 (true): all numbers work.
tutorials.example: x + 1 = x + 2 leads to 1 = 2, no solution
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what does no solution mean in an equation'.

triggers: how do you graph a linear inequality with two variables
what does a shaded region mean
tutorials.title: Graphing Two-Variable Inequalities
tutorials.body:
For an inequality like y < 2x + 1, first graph the boundary line. Use a dashed line for < or > and a solid line for <= or >=. Then shade the side that makes the inequality true — test a point like (0, 0).

Example: y < 2x + 1. Draw a dashed line y = 2x + 1. Test (0,0): 0 < 1 is true, so shade the side containing (0, 0).
tutorials.example: y >= x: solid line, shade above
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you graph a linear inequality with two variables'.

tutorials.title: Direct Variation
tutorials.body:
Direct variation means two quantities grow together at a constant rate: y = kx, where k is the constant of variation. As x doubles, y doubles. Its graph is a straight line through the origin.

Example: if y = 3x, then k = 3. When x = 2, y = 6; when x = 4, y = 12. To find k, divide y by x for any matching pair.
tutorials.example: y = 5x is direct variation with k = 5
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is direct variation'.

tutorials.title: Inverse Variation
tutorials.body:
Inverse variation means as one quantity goes up, the other goes down so their product stays constant: y = k/x, or xy = k. Its graph is a curve, not a line.

Example: y = 12/x. When x = 2, y = 6; when x = 4, y = 3 — x doubled and y halved, but xy = 12 each time. Speed and travel time vary inversely for a fixed distance.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is inverse variation'.

triggers: what is the constant of proportionality
how do you find the constant of proportionality
tutorials.title: Constant of Proportionality
tutorials.body:
In a proportional relationship y = kx, the number k is the constant of proportionality — it tells how much y changes per unit of x. Find it by dividing y by x for any pair.

Example: a table shows x: 2,3,4 and y: 6,9,12. Each y/x = 3, so k = 3 and the rule is y = 3x. It's the same idea as unit rate or slope.
tutorials.example: if y = 21 when x = 7, then k = 3
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the constant of proportionality'.

tutorials.title: Exponential Growth
tutorials.body:
Exponential growth multiplies by the same factor each step instead of adding. It looks like y = a times b^x with b greater than 1. Growth starts slow then explodes.

Example: a population that doubles each year: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. The rule is y = 1 times 2^x. Compare to linear, which would add the same amount each time, not multiply.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is exponential growth'.

tutorials.title: Exponential Decay
tutorials.body:
Exponential decay multiplies by a factor between 0 and 1 each step, so the amount shrinks fast at first then levels off. The form is y = a times b^x with 0 < b < 1.

Example: medicine that halves each hour starting at 100 mg: 100, 50, 25, 12.5. The rule is y = 100 times (1/2)^x. The factor 1/2 makes it decay.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is exponential decay'.

triggers: what are the zeros of a function
how do you find the zeros
tutorials.title: Zeros of a Function
tutorials.body:
The zeros of a function are the inputs that make the output equal zero — exactly where the graph crosses the x-axis. To find them, set f(x) = 0 and solve. They're also called roots or x-intercepts.

Example: f(x) = x^2 - 9. Set it to zero: x^2 - 9 = 0, so x = 3 or x = -3. Those are the two zeros, where the parabola hits the x-axis.
tutorials.example: f(x) = x - 4 has zero at x = 4
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what are the zeros of a function'.

triggers: what is end behavior of a function
how do you describe end behavior
tutorials.title: End Behavior
tutorials.body:
End behavior describes what a graph does at its far left and far right — does it shoot up, fall down, or level off as x goes to very large or very small values?

Example: f(x) = x^2 rises on both ends (both arms point up). f(x) = -x^2 falls on both ends. A line with positive slope falls on the left and rises on the right.
tutorials.example: y = x^3 falls left, rises right
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is end behavior of a function'.

triggers: how do you shift a graph
what is a vertical and horizontal shift
tutorials.title: Shifting Graphs
tutorials.body:
Adding outside the function moves the graph up or down; changing inside moves it left or right (and inside works backwards). For f(x): f(x) + k shifts up k, f(x) - k shifts down. f(x - h) shifts right h, f(x + h) shifts left.

Example: y = x^2 + 3 lifts the parabola up 3. y = (x - 2)^2 slides it right 2. Inside shifts feel reversed, so x - 2 means move right.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you shift a graph'.

triggers: how do you reflect a graph
what is a reflection of a graph
tutorials.title: Reflecting Graphs
tutorials.body:
A negative sign flips a graph over an axis. -f(x) flips it over the x-axis (upside down). f(-x) flips it over the y-axis (left-right mirror).

Example: y = x^2 opens up; y = -x^2 flips to open down. For y = square root of x, replacing x with -x mirrors it across the y-axis. The minus sign placement decides the axis.
tutorials.example: y = -x^2 is y = x^2 flipped down
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you reflect a graph'.

triggers: how do you stretch a graph
tutorials.title: Stretching and Compressing Graphs
tutorials.body:
Multiplying a function by a number changes its steepness. a times f(x) with a > 1 stretches it taller (steeper); with 0 < a < 1 it squishes it shorter (wider).

Example: y = 2x^2 is a narrower, steeper parabola than y = x^2. y = (1/2)x^2 is a wider, flatter one. The bigger the multiplier, the steeper the curve.
tutorials.example: y = 3x^2 is steeper than y = x^2
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you stretch a graph'.

triggers: what is an absolute value function
tutorials.title: Absolute Value Functions
tutorials.body:
The absolute value function f(x) = |x| makes a V-shape because it turns every output positive. The point of the V (the vertex) sits where the inside equals zero.

Example: f(x) = |x| has its vertex at (0, 0) and both arms go up at slope 1 and -1. f(x) = |x - 3| moves the V's point to (3, 0).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is an absolute value function'.

triggers: what is a square root function
tutorials.title: Square Root Functions
tutorials.body:
The square root function f(x) = square root of x makes a curve that starts at a point and rises slowly, like half a sideways parabola. Its domain is x >= 0 because you can't take the square root of a negative (in real numbers).

Example: f(x) = square root of x passes through (0,0), (1,1), (4,2), (9,3). The outputs grow but slower and slower.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a square root function'.

tutorials.title: Cubic Functions
tutorials.body:
A cubic function has x-cubed as its highest power: f(x) = ax^3 + ... Its basic graph (y = x^3) makes an S-shaped curve that falls on the left and rises on the right, passing through the origin.

Example: f(x) = x^3 gives -8, -1, 0, 1, 8 for x = -2,-1,0,1,2. Unlike a parabola, it keeps going down on one side and up on the other.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a cubic function'.

tutorials.title: What a Polynomial Is
tutorials.body:
A polynomial is a sum of terms made of numbers and variables raised to whole-number powers. No variables in denominators, under roots, or with negative exponents. The pieces are monomial (1 term), binomial (2), trinomial (3).

Example: 3x^2 + 2x - 5 is a polynomial (a trinomial). But 4/x or x^(1/2) are NOT polynomials because of the negative/fractional powers.
tutorials.example: x^3 + x is a polynomial; 1/x is not
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is a polynomial'.

triggers: what is the degree of a polynomial
how do you find the degree
tutorials.title: Degree of a Polynomial
tutorials.body:
The degree of a polynomial is the highest exponent on the variable. It controls the shape and the most an expression can be. The term with that exponent is the leading term.

Example: 4x^3 + 2x^2 - x + 7 has degree 3 (from x^3). A plain number like 8 has degree 0. The degree tells you the maximum number of solutions a polynomial equation can have.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the degree of a polynomial'.

tutorials.title: Adding Polynomials
tutorials.body:
To add polynomials, combine like terms — add the coefficients of terms that share the same variable and power. Line them up by power to stay organized.

Example: (3x^2 + 2x + 1) + (x^2 + 5x + 4). Add x^2 terms: 4x^2. Add x terms: 7x. Add constants: 5. Result: 4x^2 + 7x + 5.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you add polynomials'.

tutorials.title: Subtracting Polynomials
tutorials.body:
To subtract polynomials, distribute the minus sign to every term in the second polynomial (flip all its signs), then combine like terms.

Example: (5x^2 + 3x) - (2x^2 - x). Flip the second: -2x^2 + x. Now add: (5x^2 - 2x^2) + (3x + x) = 3x^2 + 4x. Forgetting to flip every sign is the most common mistake.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you subtract polynomials'.

triggers: how do you multiply two binomials
tutorials.title: Multiplying Binomials (FOIL)
tutorials.body:
FOIL is a way to multiply two binomials: First, Outer, Inner, Last. Multiply those four pairs, then combine like terms.

Example: (x + 2)(x + 3). First: x times x = x^2. Outer: x times 3 = 3x. Inner: 2 times x = 2x. Last: 2 times 3 = 6. Combine: x^2 + 5x + 6.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is foil'.

triggers: how do you multiply a monomial by a polynomial
explain multiplying a term by a polynomial
tutorials.title: Multiplying a Monomial by a Polynomial
tutorials.body:
Distribute the single term to every term inside the parentheses, multiplying coefficients and adding exponents on matching variables.

Example: 2x(3x + 4). Multiply: 2x times 3x = 6x^2, and 2x times 4 = 8x. Result: 6x^2 + 8x. Remember the exponent rule: x times x = x^2.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you multiply a monomial by a polynomial'.

tutorials.title: Adding and Subtracting Radicals
tutorials.body:
You can only add or subtract radicals that have the same root inside (like radicals), the same way you combine like terms. Add the numbers in front and keep the radical.

Example: 2 times square root of 3 plus 4 times square root of 3 = 6 times square root of 3. But square root of 2 + square root of 3 can't combine — different radicands. Simplify first so hidden like radicals appear.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you add radicals'.

triggers: how to multiply two square roots
tutorials.title: Multiplying Radicals
tutorials.body:
To multiply square roots, multiply what's inside and keep one radical: square root of a times square root of b = square root of (a times b). Then simplify if you can.

Example: square root of 2 times square root of 8 = square root of 16 = 4. And square root of 3 times square root of 12 = square root of 36 = 6. Simplifying after multiplying often gives a clean number.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you multiply radicals'.

triggers: what is the index of a radical

what does the small number on a root mean
tutorials.title: The Index of a Radical
tutorials.body:
The index is the little number tucked into a radical sign that tells which root to take. No number means 2 (square root). A 3 means cube root, a 4 means fourth root, and so on.

Example: cube root of 27 = 3 because 3 times 3 times 3 = 27. Fourth root of 16 = 2 because 2^4 = 16. The index asks 'what number, used that many times, gives this?'
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the index of a radical'.

triggers: how do you solve a proportion
tutorials.title: Solving Proportions
tutorials.body:
A proportion sets two ratios equal: a/b = c/d. Solve it by cross multiplying — multiply diagonally and set the products equal, then solve for the unknown.

Example: x/4 = 6/8. Cross multiply: 8x = 24, so x = 3. Proportions solve scaling problems like recipes, maps, and similar shapes.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you solve a proportion'.

triggers: how do you write an expression from words
how to turn a sentence into an equation
tutorials.title: Translating Words to Algebra
tutorials.body:
Turn key words into operations: 'sum/more than' is +, 'difference/less than' is -, 'product/times' is x, 'quotient/per' is divide. 'Is/equals' becomes =. Pick a letter for the unknown.

Example: 'five more than twice a number' becomes 2n + 5. 'A number decreased by 7 is 12' becomes n - 7 = 12. Watch order: 'less than' flips it (3 less than n is n - 3).
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you write an expression from words'.

triggers: how do you solve consecutive integer problems
what are consecutive integers in algebra
tutorials.title: Consecutive Integer Problems
tutorials.body:
Consecutive integers go in a row, so name them n, n+1, n+2. For consecutive even or odd integers, step by 2: n, n+2, n+4. Then write an equation from the clue.

Example: three consecutive integers sum to 36. Write n + (n+1) + (n+2) = 36, so 3n + 3 = 36, 3n = 33, n = 11. The integers are 11, 12, 13.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you solve consecutive integer problems'.

triggers: how do you square a binomial
what is the square of a binomial
tutorials.title: Squaring a Binomial
tutorials.body:
Squaring a binomial means multiplying it by itself: (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2. Don't just square each term — the middle 2ab is essential. A common mistake is writing a^2 + b^2.

Example: (x + 3)^2 = x^2 + 2(x)(3) + 9 = x^2 + 6x + 9. And (x - 4)^2 = x^2 - 8x + 16.

triggers: what is the difference between a function and a relation
tutorials.title: Function vs Relation
tutorials.body:
A relation is any set of ordered pairs linking inputs to outputs. A function is a special relation where each input has exactly one output. So every function is a relation, but not every relation is a function.

Example: {(1,2), (3,4), (5,6)} is a function — no repeated inputs. But {(1,2), (1,5)} is only a relation, because input 1 has two outputs.
tutorials.example: {(2,3),(2,7)} is a relation, not a function

triggers: how does the inverse property work
tutorials.title: Inverse Properties
tutorials.body:
An inverse undoes a number back to the identity. The additive inverse (opposite) of a is -a, since a + (-a) = 0. The multiplicative inverse (reciprocal) of a is 1/a, since a times 1/a = 1.

Example: the opposite of 6 is -6 (6 + -6 = 0). The reciprocal of 4 is 1/4 (4 times 1/4 = 1). These power the rules for solving equations.
tutorials.example: opposite of -3 is 3; reciprocal of 5 is 1/5
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the inverse property'.

triggers: how do you simplify a rational expression
how to reduce a fraction with variables
tutorials.title: Simplifying Rational Expressions
tutorials.body:
A rational expression is a fraction with polynomials. To simplify, factor the top and bottom, then cancel any common factors — just like reducing a numeric fraction.

Example: (x^2 - 9)/(x + 3). Factor the top: (x + 3)(x - 3). Cancel the (x + 3): you're left with x - 3. You can only cancel whole factors, never individual terms.

triggers: when is a rational expression undefined
tutorials.title: When a Rational Expression Is Undefined
tutorials.body:
A fraction is undefined when its denominator equals zero, because dividing by zero has no meaning. For a rational expression, find which x-values make the bottom zero and exclude them.

Example: in 5/(x - 2), the expression is undefined at x = 2 (that makes the bottom zero). For 1/(x^2 - 9), it's undefined at x = 3 and x = -3.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'when is a rational expression undefined'.

triggers: how do you find both intercepts of a line
explain finding x and y intercepts
tutorials.title: Graphing With Intercepts
tutorials.body:
You can graph a line fast using just its two intercepts. Set y = 0 to get the x-intercept, set x = 0 to get the y-intercept, plot both points, and connect them.

Example: 2x + 3y = 12. x-intercept (y=0): x = 6, point (6,0). y-intercept (x=0): y = 4, point (0,4). Draw the line through (6,0) and (0,4).

triggers: what are the basic function families
tutorials.title: Parent Functions
tutorials.body:
A parent function is the simplest form of a function family, before any shifts or stretches. Learning the parent's shape lets you predict every transformed version. Common ones: y = x (line), y = x^2 (parabola), y = |x| (V), y = square root of x (curve), y = x^3 (S-curve).

Example: y = (x - 3)^2 + 1 is the parent y = x^2 moved right 3 and up 1. Knowing the parent shape makes graphing fast.

triggers: how is slope a unit rate
why is slope like price per item
tutorials.title: Slope as a Unit Rate
tutorials.body:
In real-world linear relationships, the slope is a unit rate — how much one thing changes per single unit of another. It carries units like dollars per hour or miles per gallon.

Example: if a job pays $45 for 3 hours, the slope (pay per hour) is 45/3 = $15 per hour. The equation y = 15x predicts pay for any hours x.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how is slope a unit rate'.

triggers: how do you write a line through two points
explain finding the equation from two points
how to get y = mx + b from two points
tutorials.title: Equation From Two Points
tutorials.body:
Given two points, first find the slope, then use one point to find the y-intercept. Plug into y = mx + b.

Example: points (1, 3) and (3, 7). Slope = (7 - 3)/(3 - 1) = 2. Use (1, 3): 3 = 2(1) + b, so b = 1. The equation is y = 2x + 1.
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'how do you write a line through two points'.

triggers: what is the difference between recursive and explicit formulas
tutorials.title: Recursive vs Explicit Formulas
tutorials.body:
A recursive formula builds each term from the one before (you need the previous term). An explicit formula computes any term directly from its position number. Explicit is faster for far-out terms.

Example: for 3, 5, 7, 9... recursive is 'next = previous + 2'. Explicit is a(n) = 2n + 1, so the 10th term is 2(10) + 1 = 21 without listing them all.
tutorials.example: explicit a(n) = 3n finds the 100th term fast
tutorials.tryIt: Try: ask me 'what is the difference between recursive and explicit formulas'.

tutorials.title: Arithmetic Sequences
tutorials.body:
An arithmetic sequence adds the same number (the common difference) each step. Its explicit rule is a(n) = a1 + (n - 1)d, where a1 is the first term and d is the difference. They graph as evenly spaced points on a line.

Example: 4, 7, 10, 13... has d = 3, a1 = 4. The rule a(n) = 4 + (n - 1)3. The 6th term: 4 + 5(3) = 19.

tutorials.title: Geometric Sequences
tutorials.body:
A geometric sequence multiplies by the same number (the common ratio) each step. Its explicit rule is a(n) = a1 times r^(n-1). Geometric sequences grow or shrink exponentially.

Example: 3, 6, 12, 24... has ratio r = 2, a1 = 3. Rule: a(n) = 3 times 2^(n-1). The 5th term: 3 times 2^4 = 48.

tutorials.title: Arithmetic vs Geometric
tutorials.body:
To classify a sequence, check the pattern between terms. If you ADD the same amount each time, it's arithmetic (common difference). If you MULTIPLY by the same amount, it's geometric (common ratio).

Example: 5, 10, 15, 20 adds 5 each time (arithmetic). But 5, 10, 20, 40 multiplies by 2 each time (geometric). Look at whether successive differences or successive ratios are constant.
