tutorials.title: Absolute Value Inequalities
tutorials.body:
Split an absolute value inequality into two parts. For |x| < c (less-than), it becomes -c < x < c (a sandwich). For |x| > c (greater-than), it becomes x < -c OR x > c (two outer pieces).

Example: |x| < 4 means -4 < x < 4. But |x| > 4 means x < -4 or x > 4. Less-than is 'and' (between), greater-than is 'or' (outside).

tutorials.title: Average Rate of Change
tutorials.body:
For a curve, the average rate of change between two points is the slope of the line connecting them: (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a). It tells the overall climb between those inputs, even if the curve wiggles.

Example: f(x) = x^2 from x=1 to x=3. f(1)=1, f(3)=9. Average rate = (9 - 1)/(3 - 1) = 8/2 = 4. On a straight line this just equals the constant slope.

how to put an equation in y = form
tutorials.title: Solving an Equation for y
tutorials.body:
To rewrite an equation in y = form, isolate y on one side using inverse operations. This makes it easy to graph or find the slope and intercept.

Example: 2x + y = 8. Subtract 2x: y = -2x + 8 (slope -2, intercept 8). With 3x - 2y = 6: subtract 3x, then divide by -2: y = (3/2)x - 3.

tutorials.title: Maximum and Minimum of a Quadratic
tutorials.body:
Every parabola has one turning point at its vertex. If it opens up (positive a), the vertex is the minimum. If it opens down (negative a), the vertex is the maximum. The y-value of the vertex is that extreme value.

Example: f(x) = -x^2 + 4x. It opens down, so it has a maximum. Vertex x = -4/(2 times -1) = 2, and f(2) = 4. The maximum value is 4.
tutorials.example: y = x^2 + 2 has a minimum value of 2

tutorials.title: Interval Notation
tutorials.body:
Interval notation describes a range of numbers with brackets and parentheses. Square brackets [ ] include the endpoint; parentheses ( ) exclude it. Infinity always gets a parenthesis.

Example: x >= 2 is [2, infinity). 1 < x <= 5 is (1, 5]. All real numbers is (-infinity, infinity). It's a compact alternative to inequality notation.

how to solve x^2 + bx + c = 0
tutorials.title: Solving Quadratics by Factoring
tutorials.body:
To solve a quadratic by factoring, first get one side equal to zero, factor the other side, then set each factor equal to zero (zero product property) and solve.

Example: x^2 + x - 6 = 0. Factor: (x + 3)(x - 2) = 0. So x + 3 = 0 (x = -3) or x - 2 = 0 (x = 2). The two solutions are -3 and 2.

tutorials.title: Factoring by Grouping
tutorials.body:
Factoring by grouping works on four-term polynomials. Group them into two pairs, factor the GCF from each pair, and if the leftover binomials match, factor that out.

Example: x^3 + 2x^2 + 3x + 6. Group: x^2(x + 2) + 3(x + 2). Both have (x + 2), so factor it out: (x + 2)(x^2 + 3).

tutorials.title: The Leading Coefficient
tutorials.body:
The leading coefficient is the number in front of the term with the highest power. It controls a graph's overall direction and steepness. For a polynomial, write it in order of powers first, then read the front number.

Example: in -2x^3 + 5x - 1, the leading coefficient is -2. Its negative sign makes a cubic fall on the right, and its size makes the curve steep.

tutorials.title: Rewriting Radicals as Exponents
tutorials.body:
Any radical can be written as a fractional exponent: the nth root of x to the m power is x^(m/n). The root becomes the denominator, the power becomes the numerator. This lets you use exponent rules on radicals.

Example: square root of x is x^(1/2). The cube root of x^2 is x^(2/3). Now square root of x times square root of x = x^(1/2) times x^(1/2) = x^1 = x.

tutorials.title: What the Sign of Slope Means
tutorials.body:
The sign of slope tells the direction a line travels left to right. Positive slope rises (goes uphill). Negative slope falls (goes downhill). Zero slope is flat, and undefined slope is straight up and down.

Example: y = 2x + 1 climbs (positive). y = -3x + 4 drops (negative). The bigger the number, the steeper the climb or fall.

tutorials.title: Rearranging Geometry Formulas
tutorials.body:
Geometry formulas are literal equations you can solve for any variable. Use inverse operations the same as with numbers, treating the other letters as constants.

Example: area of a triangle A = (1/2)bh. Solve for h: multiply both sides by 2 (2A = bh), then divide by b (h = 2A/b). Now you can find a height from a known area and base.

tutorials.title: Equation From a Table
tutorials.body:
To get a linear equation from a table, find the slope (the constant change in y per step in x), then find b by reading the y-value when x = 0 (or back-solving).

Example: x: 0,1,2 and y: 4,7,10. Each y rises by 3, so slope = 3. At x = 0, y = 4, so b = 4. Equation: y = 3x + 4.

tutorials.title: One-Step Inequalities
tutorials.body:
A one-step inequality needs a single inverse operation to isolate the variable, just like a one-step equation. The catch: flip the sign if you multiply or divide by a negative.

Example: x + 4 < 9. Subtract 4: x < 5. And -2x >= 6: divide by -2 and flip: x <= -3. Adding or subtracting never flips the sign.

tutorials.title: Writing Inequalities From Words
tutorials.body:
Phrases map to inequality symbols: 'at least' and 'no less than' mean >=, 'at most' and 'no more than' mean <=, 'more than' is >, 'less than' is <. Pick a variable and translate.

Example: 'You must be at least 13 to sign up.' Let a be age: a >= 13. 'No more than 20 students' becomes s <= 20. The 'at least/at most' phrases include the boundary.

tutorials.title: Solving Exponential Equations With Like Bases
tutorials.body:
If both sides of an exponential equation can be written with the same base, set the exponents equal and solve. Rewrite numbers as powers first.

Example: 2^x = 8. Since 8 = 2^3, the equation is 2^x = 2^3, so x = 3. Another: 3^(x+1) = 27 = 3^3, so x + 1 = 3, x = 2.

tutorials.title: Identifying the Function Family
tutorials.body:
Spot the family by the pattern in a table or the equation's form. Linear adds a constant (constant first differences). Quadratic has constant second differences. Exponential multiplies by a constant ratio.

Example: y: 2,4,6,8 adds 2 (linear). y: 1,4,9,16 has first differences 3,5,7 and constant second differences 2 (quadratic). y: 2,6,18,54 multiplies by 3 (exponential).

tutorials.title: One-to-One Functions
tutorials.body:
A one-to-one function never repeats an output — each y comes from only one x. You can test it with the horizontal line test: if no horizontal line hits the graph more than once, it's one-to-one. Only one-to-one functions have true inverses.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1 is one-to-one (a slanted line passes the test). But f(x) = x^2 is not, because both x = 2 and x = -2 give 4.
tutorials.example: y = x^3 is one-to-one; y = x^2 is not

triggers: why is slope undefined for a vertical line
what happens to slope when the run is zero
tutorials.title: Why Vertical Slope Is Undefined
tutorials.body:
Slope is rise over run. A vertical line has two points with the same x-value, so the run (change in x) is zero. Since dividing by zero is undefined, the slope is undefined — not zero.

Example: line through (3, 1) and (3, 6). Slope = (6 - 1)/(3 - 3) = 5/0, which is undefined. The line just goes straight up, so 'steepness as a number' doesn't exist.

what happens to signs inside parentheses
tutorials.title: Distributing a Negative Sign
tutorials.body:
A minus sign in front of parentheses flips the sign of every term inside, because it's really multiplying by -1.

Example: -(x - 4) = -x + 4 (both signs flip). And 5 - (2x - 3) = 5 - 2x + 3 = -2x + 8. Forgetting to flip the second term's sign is one of the most common algebra slips.

tutorials.title: Domain Restrictions From Division
tutorials.body:
When a function has a variable in the denominator, the domain excludes any x that makes the denominator zero, since division by zero is undefined. Find those forbidden x-values by setting the denominator to zero.

Example: f(x) = 1/(x - 5). The denominator is zero at x = 5, so the domain is all real numbers except 5. For 1/(x^2 - 4), exclude x = 2 and x = -2.

tutorials.title: Simplifying Complex Fractions
tutorials.body:
A complex fraction has fractions inside its top or bottom. Simplify by remembering a fraction bar means division: divide the top by the bottom, which means multiply by the reciprocal.

Example: (1/2)/(3/4). This is 1/2 divided by 3/4, so flip and multiply: 1/2 times 4/3 = 4/6 = 2/3. Treat the big bar as 'divided by'.

tutorials.title: Graphing From Slope-Intercept Form
tutorials.body:
To graph y = mx + b, plot the y-intercept b first as a point on the y-axis. Then use the slope as rise over run to step to another point, and draw the line.

Example: y = (2/3)x - 1. Start at (0, -1). Slope 2/3 means up 2, right 3, landing at (3, 1). Connect the two points and extend.

tutorials.title: Two-Step Inequalities
tutorials.body:
Solve a two-step inequality just like a two-step equation: undo addition/subtraction first, then multiplication/division. Flip the sign only if you divide or multiply by a negative.

Example: 3x - 5 < 7. Add 5: 3x < 12. Divide by 3: x < 4. But -2x + 1 > 9: subtract 1 (-2x > 8), divide by -2 and flip (x < -4).

tutorials.title: Power of a Product
tutorials.body:
When a product is raised to a power, the exponent applies to each factor: (xy)^n = x^n times y^n. The same goes for numbers and coefficients inside.

Example: (3x)^2 = 3^2 times x^2 = 9x^2. And (2ab)^3 = 2^3 a^3 b^3 = 8a^3 b^3. Don't forget to raise the number out front to the power too.

triggers: what is the power of a quotient rule

tutorials.title: Power of a Quotient
tutorials.body:
When a fraction is raised to a power, raise both the top and bottom to that power: (x/y)^n = x^n / y^n.

Example: (x/3)^2 = x^2 / 9. And (2/y)^3 = 8 / y^3. It's the quotient version of the power-of-a-product rule, applied to numerator and denominator separately.

how to move a V graph
tutorials.title: Shifting Absolute Value Graphs
tutorials.body:
The V-shaped graph of f(x) = |x - h| + k has its corner (vertex) at (h, k). The inside number moves it left/right (backwards), the outside number moves it up/down.

Example: y = |x - 2| + 3. The vertex is at (2, 3) — right 2 and up 3 from the basic V. A negative inside like |x + 1| moves it left 1.

tutorials.title: What a Monomial Is
tutorials.body:
A monomial is a single term: a number, a variable, or numbers and variables multiplied together with whole-number exponents. No plus or minus signs joining pieces, no division by a variable.

Example: 5, x, 3x^2, and -7ab are all monomials. But x + 2 (two terms) and 4/x (variable in denominator) are not. Monomials are the building blocks of polynomials.

tutorials.title: Dividing Monomials
tutorials.body:
To divide monomials, divide the coefficients and subtract the exponents of matching variables (the quotient rule).

Example: 12x^5 / 4x^2. Divide numbers: 12/4 = 3. Subtract exponents: x^(5-2) = x^3. Result: 3x^3. If the variable cancels completely (same exponent), it becomes x^0 = 1.

how to get rid of denominators
tutorials.title: Clearing Fractions From Equations
tutorials.body:
To solve an equation with fractions, multiply every term by the least common denominator. This clears all fractions, leaving a simpler whole-number equation.

Example: x/2 + 1/3 = 5/6. The LCD is 6. Multiply each term by 6: 3x + 2 = 5. Then 3x = 3, x = 1. Multiplying the WHOLE equation keeps it balanced.
